title: Epidemic Modeling
book: T. Lazebnik, Epidemic Modeling: Principles, Algorithms, and Applications (Academic Press, 2026)
description: A free course on how to describe epidemics with mathematics and computation: history, compartmental and spatial models, strains, agent-based simulation, data-driven forecasting, calibration, surveillance data, interventions, uncertainty and computing. Short animated episodes, slides, labs and games.

book_parts.author: Teddy Lazebnik
book_parts.title: Epidemic Modeling: Principles, Algorithms, and Applications

modules.title: History of pandemics and modeling
modules.sub: From the plague of Athens to COVID-19, and how models grew up

games.why: steer a city through an SIR epidemic and feel the trade-offs between mobility, testing and protection that the course turns into models.

modules.summary: Why study history before models? Every pandemic is the same basic story, but four things change from one to the next: how people are connected, how they live, what they believe causes the disease, and what tools they have. We visit Athens, the Black Death, quarantine and cholera; take one lesson for modelers from each modern pandemic, from the 1918 flu to COVID-19; and follow modeling from counting deaths to the SIR model, our first simulation and the model families of this course.
modules.goal: name the four background conditions that shape an outbreak, give one modeling lesson from each modern pandemic, and explain the epidemic threshold.

modules.title: Beyond the virus
modules.summary: An epidemic is more than a virus. We treat spread as a tug of war between transmission and interruption, see why the reproduction number depends on the setting, why uneven spread makes outbreaks rarer but more explosive, and why data lags behind reality; then the biology underneath (pathogens, the three clocks of infection, routes, immunity, spillover), the psychology and economics of how people react, and the role of governments in one coupled system with feedback loops and late data.
modules.goal: explain why R depends on the setting, show how timing in the body and in policy changes outcomes, and describe the feedback loop between disease, behavior, money and policy.

modules.title: Compartmental models
modules.sub: SIR and its family, R₀ and the next-generation matrix
modules.summary: The workhorse of epidemic modeling. We build the SIR model from its assumptions, derive R0, the epidemic threshold and the final-size relation, and see why epidemics stop before everyone is infected. Then we add boxes (births and deaths, reinfection, latency, infectious stages, hospital outcomes, age groups, mosquitoes), let transmission change with seasons, interventions and behavior, bring in chance with stochastic simulation and early extinction, and finish with the next-generation matrix, the general recipe for R0.
modules.goal: write and solve an SIR-family model, compute R0 and the final size, explain early extinction in stochastic models, and build a next-generation matrix for a model with several infected types.

modules.title: Spatio-temporal models
modules.summary: Epidemics happen in places. We link cities by travel (metapopulation models), put people on contact networks, let infection spread as a wave across continuous space, and use matrix norms to bound growth without solving everything. Along the way: effective distance, imported sparks, excess degree and hubs, clustering, wave speed, borders, long jumps, transient growth and the critical patch size.
modules.goal: build a metapopulation model and read its timing, compute an epidemic threshold on a contact network, estimate the speed of an epidemic wave, and use matrix norms to prove that an outbreak dies out.

modules.title: Multi-strain and evolving pandemics
modules.summary: Most diseases come in several strains. We give each strain its own infected box in one shared pool of people, show that identical strains are just labels, see why a fitter strain must also arrive in time, and read its advantage from the log odds of its share. Then we track immune history, see the number of boxes explode, add cross-immunity and the invasion threshold, and follow strains arriving one after another into repeat waves. Finally, mutation makes new strains during the epidemic: in the equations a new strain grows smoothly from day one, in reality it starts as one case and often fizzles, and controlling spread slows evolution.
modules.goal: build a multi-strain model with immune histories, compute a new strain's effective reproduction number in the immunity landscape it meets, add mutation with a mutation matrix, and explain why chance and the number of infections decide how often new strains emerge.

modules.title: Multi-agent simulation
modules.sub: Building, running and trusting agent-based models
modules.summary: Agent-based models simulate every person. We build agents with states, rules and neighbours, check that average agents give back the SIR equations, and see what heterogeneity changes. Agents can compute anything, which costs prediction, and their contact loops cost time. Then the building blocks: time steps or events, the update order, the neighbourhood, seeds and reproducibility, common random numbers for sharp comparisons, and richer agents. We finish with two case studies in a toy town (a flu-like illness with a school closure, a COVID-like illness with isolation and behaviour), seven design steps, sensitivity analysis, and the ethics and policy risks of these models.
modules.goal: design a small agent-based epidemic model, choose its time step, update order and geometry on purpose, make it reproducible, compare policies with common random numbers, and report its uncertainty, privacy and equity issues honestly.

modules.title: Data-driven models
modules.sub: From observation models to machine-learning forecasts
modules.summary: Models built from data. On a simulated surveillance system with a known truth, we separate infections from reported cases with an observation model (overdispersion, zeros, the log scale), take weekday and holiday reporting patterns apart, forecast with seasonal ARIMA and state-space models in an honest rolling-origin backtest, correct the latest days for reporting delay with a nowcast, compare machine-learning and deep-learning forecasters with simple baselines, and use large language models carefully, as readers with fixed forms and checks.
modules.goal: choose an observation model for case counts, remove calendar effects, run a rolling-origin backtest against simple baselines, nowcast recent days from a reporting triangle, and judge when machine learning or language models add value.

modules.title: Parameter estimation and calibration
modules.sub: Fitting models to data, and knowing when you can't
modules.summary: Fitting models to data, and knowing when you can't. On one simulated outbreak with a known truth, we fit by least squares (and see why cumulative fits give false confidence), compare grid, Bayesian, genetic and swarm searches, refine with gradients, curvature and Nelder-Mead, fit models without a likelihood with approximate Bayesian computation and a particle filter, calibrate for a purpose with targets, observation mappings and losses, and diagnose identifiability and misspecification.
modules.goal: fit a model by weighted least squares, choose a search method for the problem at hand, use simulation-based inference when no likelihood exists, design a calibration around its purpose, and check identifiability with profiles and stress tests.

modules.title: Surveillance, mobility and genomic data
modules.sub: What the data streams see, and what they miss
modules.summary: What the data streams see, and what they miss. In a simulated city with a known epidemic, we treat surveillance as a measurement process (delays, a reporting share that changes), correct serosurveys for imperfect tests, see how phone-based mobility data can mislead, use genomes to follow a new variant and the bias in which samples get sequenced, and read wastewater, search and pharmacy signals, then combine the streams.
modules.goal: write the observation model behind a data stream, correct a serosurvey for test errors, judge mobility and genomic data by how they were sampled, and combine several streams to follow one hidden epidemic.

modules.title: Intervention policies

games.why: steer a city through an epidemic with your own policies, then compare your choices with the trade-offs this module computes.

modules.summary: Interventions, optimal control and vaccination. In made-up towns, we put interventions into the equations (a dial on transmission, settings in a contact matrix, vaccination as a flow, isolation as a box), see why lockdown timing matters as much as strength, solve an optimal-control problem two ways, weigh health against the economy on a Pareto front, choose who gets vaccinated first, and see how travel cuts, data lags and drug resistance change the answer.
modules.goal: write an intervention into an epidemic model, set up and solve a simple optimal-control problem, read a Pareto front without pretending it picks the answer, compare vaccine priorities for different goals, and judge trigger policies by the lag of their signal.

modules.title: Uncertainty, sensitivity and model comparison
modules.sub: Where uncertainty comes from, and how to measure it
modules.summary: Where uncertainty comes from, and how to measure it. On made-up towns with known truths, we add the sources of uncertainty one layer at a time (chance, parameters, measurement, structure, scenarios, computation), show how different parameters can tell the same story and what breaks the tie, rank inputs with local derivatives, Morris screening and Sobol indices, and compare forecasters with proper scores and interval coverage.
modules.goal: name the sources of uncertainty in a forecast, recognize confounded parameters and the data that separates them, choose and read a sensitivity analysis, and evaluate forecasts with backtests, proper scores and calibration.

modules.title: Computational considerations
modules.sub: Software, numerical stability, speed and scale
modules.summary: The computer side of epidemic modeling. With our own code and timings, we write one agent model in four languages and check that all give the same answer, keep a model's parts apart and catch a planted bug with a conservation test, see Euler's method overshoot and go negative while Runge–Kutta holds, meet stiff models and the solvers built for them, compare exact and tau-leaping stochastic simulation, speed code up by profiling, better algorithms, batching and sparse structure, and calibrate at scale with exact gradients, emulators and history matching.
modules.goal: choose tools and structure for a modeling project, test a model as well as its code, pick a solver and step size that are stable and accurate enough, find and remove the real bottleneck in slow code, and plan a calibration that the cost of a run can afford.

modules.title: Closing remarks and future directions

games.why: one last round as mayor: steer the city with everything the course has covered.

modules.summary: Where epidemic modeling goes next. We look back at what each family of models taught us, name the problems that come back whatever the model (epidemics that change as they go, data that are measurements, models that travel badly, forecasts tested the wrong way), and sketch where the field is heading: adaptive forecasts, many data streams read together, language models under strict checks, AI that helps epidemiologists, shared benchmarks and models built around decisions.
modules.goal: explain what each modeling family is good for, recognize the recurring pitfalls in any epidemic model, and judge new methods by the decisions they serve.

transcript.title: Welcome to the course
transcript.text: Welcome to Epidemic Modeling. I'm Teddy, and for the next fifty three episodes, we'll learn how to describe an epidemic with mathematics. This course follows my book, chapter by chapter. Each module is one chapter. But you don't need the book to follow along. Models come later. First, I want to show you the problem they try to solve. And the best place to see it is history.

transcript.title: Four things that change
transcript.text: Every pandemic is the same basic story: something passes from one person to another, faster than people can stop it. But the setting changes. Four things, especially. How people are connected. How they live, day to day. What they believe causes the disease. And what tools they have to fight back. Change those four, and the same germ writes a completely different story. Keep that list in mind. We'll use it all episode.

transcript.title: Athens, around 430 BC
transcript.text: Our first stop: Athens, around 430 BC, in the second year of a long war with Sparta. The strategy was simple. Bring everyone from the countryside inside the city walls, and let the navy do the fighting. So now you have a city packed with refugees, in summer, sharing water and space. Connection, turned all the way up. Then a disease arrived by sea. Fever, rash, terrible thirst. A large share of the city died, including its leader, Pericles. We know this because the historian Thucydides wrote it down. He caught the disease himself, and survived to describe it. Two and a half thousand years later, we still argue about what the disease actually was. Typhus? Smallpox? Typhoid? Nobody is sure. But Thucydides noticed something we still see today: people stopped caring for the sick, and stopped following the rules. Fear spreads too.

transcript.title: The Black Death
transcript.text: Next stop: 1347. Merchant ships reach Sicily from the Black Sea, carrying the plague. The bacterium, Yersinia pestis, travels with fleas on rats, and sometimes directly from person to person through the air. And it travels with trade. Ports first, then rivers and roads. Within about four years, it crossed most of Europe. Estimates of the toll range from about a third to more than half of Europe's population. Think about that for a second. In some towns, it was every second person you knew. Nobody knew about bacteria. The common belief was bad air, or divine punishment. And yet, people found a tool that worked.

transcript.title: Quarantine
transcript.text: In 1377, the port of Ragusa, today Dubrovnik, ordered ships and travelers from infected places to wait thirty days before entering. Venice later made it forty days. In Italian, forty is quaranta. And that's where the word quarantine comes from. Cities started health boards, health passes, and records of who died and when. Public health began as government, not as medicine. Notice what happened: they changed the connections, without knowing the cause. Sometimes you can act before you fully understand.

transcript.title: Cholera: what causes it?
transcript.text: Last stop for today: cholera. A disease that kills through dehydration, sometimes within hours. It had long been present around Bengal. In 1817, it started travelling, and over the next decades it reached Europe and the Americas. The big argument was about the cause. Bad air from filth, said one side. Something passed between people, said the other. And the answer decided the policy. Bad air means cleaning streets. Contagion means stopping people at the border.

transcript.title: John Snow's map
transcript.text: London, 1854. A doctor named John Snow marks every cholera death in one neighborhood on a map. The deaths cluster around one water pump, on Broad Street. The handle is removed, and the outbreak there was already fading. That map is one of the first great pictures in epidemiology. Data, placed in space, pointing at a cause. The same year, in Florence, Filippo Pacini saw the bacterium under a microscope. Robert Koch isolated it in 1883. And with germ theory, the tools changed. Now you could target the pathogen, not only the people.

transcript.title: Same problem, three stories
transcript.text: So, back to our list. In Athens, crowding behind walls changed how people were connected. With the plague, trade routes carried it, and quarantine was the tool, long before anyone saw a bacterium. With cholera, a new belief about the cause, backed by data, changed the tools. Same problem, three different stories. A good epidemic model has to know which story it's in.

transcript.title: Next: 1918 to COVID-19
transcript.text: Next episode: from the 1918 flu to COVID-19, a century of pandemics that looked a lot more like ours. See you there. And maybe wash your hands. Snow would approve.

episodes.title: From 1918 to COVID-19
episodes.hook: A century of pandemics that look a lot like ours: the 1918 flu, HIV, SARS, the 2009 H1N1 flu, Ebola in West Africa and COVID-19.
episodes.takeaway: Every modern pandemic left a lesson: waves, time scales, superspreading, biased early numbers, delays and trust.

transcript.title: Six pandemics
transcript.text: Last time we walked from Athens to cholera. Today: the last hundred years or so, where pandemics start to look a lot like ours. Six of them. Each one taught modelers something different. Let's go.

transcript.title: 1918 influenza
transcript.text: 1918. The First World War is ending, and a new influenza virus is spreading through armies, ships and cities. It's called the Spanish flu, but it almost certainly did not start in Spain. Spain was neutral, and its newspapers were free to report it. It came in waves. A milder one in spring, a much deadlier one in the autumn, and more outbreaks early the next year. Common estimates put the deaths around fifty million, with a wide range, because many countries kept poor records. And it was strange: many of the dead were young adults, not only the old and the very young. Lesson for modelers: an epidemic doesn't have to have one peak. Waves are normal, and the second one can be worse.

transcript.title: HIV and AIDS
transcript.text: 1981. Doctors report clusters of rare infections in young, otherwise healthy men. It's the first recognition of HIV and AIDS. HIV is slow. A person can carry it for years without symptoms, and pass it on without knowing. It spreads through sex, shared needles, blood, and from mother to child. So behavior sits at the centre of the story. More than forty million people have died of it. Since the late nineties, treatment can keep the virus in check for a lifetime. Lesson: time scales matter. A model built for a two week flu tells you nothing about a disease that unfolds over a decade.

transcript.title: SARS, 2002-03
transcript.text: November 2002, southern China. A new coronavirus causes a severe pneumonia. We call it SARS. In February 2003, one infected traveler stays at a hotel in Hong Kong. Other guests carry the virus to several countries within days. Hospitals become hot spots. Health workers are a big share of the cases. The World Health Organization counted about eight thousand cases, and nearly eight hundred deaths. By July 2003, it was contained. No vaccine, no drug. Isolation, contact tracing, and quarantine did it. Old tools, used fast.

transcript.title: H1N1, 2009
transcript.text: 2009. A new H1N1 influenza virus appears in Mexico and the United States, mixing genes from several flu lineages. By June, the World Health Organization calls it a pandemic. The first flu pandemic of this century. Early on, nobody knew how deadly it was. The first numbers came from hospitals, which see the sickest cases first. It turned out milder than many feared. Lesson: early estimates are noisy, and they're biased toward severe cases.

transcript.title: Ebola, 2013-16
transcript.text: December 2013, a village in Guinea. A small child falls ill with Ebola. Months pass before anyone recognizes the outbreak. By then, it has reached Liberia and Sierra Leone, and their capital cities. Ebola had never spread like this before. Over two years: more than twenty eight thousand cases, and more than eleven thousand deaths. Care for the sick and traditional burials put families in contact with the virus. Changing that needed trust, not only orders. Lesson: the delay between the first case and the first alarm can decide everything. And people's trust is part of the model.

transcript.title: COVID-19
transcript.text: And then, late 2019, Wuhan. A new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2. On the eleventh of March 2020, the World Health Organization calls it a pandemic. Lockdowns, masks, school closures, travel bans. Testing at a scale nobody had tried before. Vaccines arrived in about a year, including the first approved mRNA vaccines. Official reports counted around seven million deaths. Studies of excess deaths suggest the true toll was about two to three times higher. And for the first time, epidemic models were on the front page. Every day. Sometimes right, sometimes wrong, always argued about.

transcript.title: What changed, what stayed
transcript.text: So what changed over this century? Connections: planes instead of ships. A virus can cross the world in a day. Tools: vaccines, drugs, genome sequencing, and computers fast enough to simulate whole countries. And data. From almost none in 1918, to daily dashboards in 2020. But the hard parts stayed. Waves, delays, hidden cases, and people who react to the epidemic while it happens.

transcript.title: Next: how modeling grew up
transcript.text: Next episode: how epidemic modeling itself grew up, from counting deaths in London to the families of models we'll use in this course. That's where the mathematics starts. Bring a pencil.

episodes.title: How epidemic modeling grew up
episodes.hook: How epidemic modeling grew up: John Graunt counts deaths in 1662, Daniel Bernoulli builds a smallpox policy model in 1760, Farr and Snow turn data into curves and maps, and Kermack and McKendrick write the SIR model in 1927.
episodes.takeaway: From counting deaths to SIR: new infections follow meetings, and R0 = 1 is the threshold.

transcript.title: Before germs
transcript.text: The first epidemic model was written more than a hundred years before anyone knew what a germ was. Today, the story of how modeling grew up. And at the end, a map of the model families we'll use for the rest of the course.

transcript.title: Graunt counts deaths, 1662
transcript.text: Start in London, 1662. A shopkeeper called John Graunt reads the weekly bills of mortality: lists of who died, and of what. Nobody had really added them up before. Graunt did, and found patterns. Which causes grow, which seasons are worse, how plague years stand out. That's the first step of every model, even today: count carefully, and compare.

transcript.title: Bernoulli's smallpox model, 1760
transcript.text: Then, 1760. The mathematician Daniel Bernoulli asks a policy question about smallpox. Inoculation protected people, but it was risky. A small share of the inoculated died. So, is it worth it for a whole population? Bernoulli wrote equations for how many people stay susceptible as they age, and how many die of smallpox along the way. His answer: inoculating everyone at birth would add about three years to life expectancy. Worth it. Notice the shape: a model, a policy question, and a number to help decide. That's still the job.

transcript.title: Farr's curves, Snow's map
transcript.text: In the 1800s, cholera pushed governments to measure. William Farr, in England, turned death registers into curves, and tried to predict their rise and fall. And John Snow, as we saw last time, put deaths on a map and found the pump. Counting, plus place, plus a hypothesis.

transcript.title: Mass action and the threshold
transcript.text: Early 1900s, the big idea arrives: new infections depend on how often susceptible and infected people meet. William Hamer used it for measles in 1906. Ronald Ross used it for malaria, and showed you don't need to kill every mosquito, only enough of them. In 1927, Kermack and McKendrick wrote the model at the heart of this course. People are susceptible, infected, or removed. And they found a threshold. If each case infects fewer than one new person on average, the epidemic dies out. More than one, and it takes off. We'll spend the whole of Module three on that idea. It's called R naught, and you'll be sick of it. Pun intended.

transcript.title: Our SIR run
transcript.text: Here is our own small run of that model. Each infected person passes it on at a rate of three tenths per day, and recovers after ten days, on average. That makes R naught three. The infections rise, peak around day forty, and fall. About ninety four percent of the town is infected by the end. Now lower the transmission so that R naught is below one. Same town, same start. The outbreak fizzles right away. Three letters, two equations, and already a policy message: push R below one.

transcript.title: Surveillance, computers, new data
transcript.text: After the Second World War, surveillance became an institution. Countries and agencies collected disease reports every week, in the same format. Computers made it possible to simulate thousands, then millions, of individuals instead of a few equations. And this century added new data: search queries, phone mobility, wastewater, and virus genomes, read in days. New data doesn't replace the old questions, though. Who is missing from it? How biased is it? Who agreed to share it?

transcript.title: The model families
transcript.text: So today, epidemic modeling is a family of approaches. Here's the map for this course. Compartmental models put people into groups, like susceptible, infected, recovered. Clear and fast, but they treat everyone in a group as the same. Spatial and network models add where people are, and who meets whom. Agent-based models simulate every person, with their own home, job and habits. Realistic, but hungry for data and computer time. Data-driven and machine learning models learn patterns straight from the numbers. Good at short-term forecasts, weaker at explaining why. None of them is the best. Each one is the right tool for some question. Choosing well is half the skill.

transcript.title: The road ahead
transcript.text: The course follows that map. Next comes Module two, the world around the virus: biology, psychology, economics and government. Then compartmental models, space, strains, agents, data, calibration, surveillance, interventions, uncertainty, and computing. That's history done. From here on, we build. See you in Module two.

episodes.title: How infections spread, and the biology behind it
episodes.hook: Two viruses can look almost the same and still write very different epidemics.
episodes.takeaway: R depends on the setting: who meets whom, uneven spread, delays, and the order of the body’s clocks.

transcript.title: Same virus, different epidemics
transcript.text: Two viruses can look almost the same in a clinic, and still write completely different epidemics. This module is about why. Module two is everything beyond the virus itself. Today: how infections spread through a population, and the biology underneath.

transcript.title: Transmission vs interruption
transcript.text: Think of an epidemic as a tug of war. On one side, transmission: an infectious person meets a susceptible one, and the germ gets across. On the other side, interruption: people become immune, cases are isolated sooner, or contacts change. We sum up the balance with one number, the reproduction number: how many people one typical case goes on to infect. At 1.5, one case grows to about eleven in six generations. At 0.7, the same chain shrinks to almost nothing. And that number is not a property of the virus alone. It depends on how people mix, how fast cases are found, and what is in place to stop them.

transcript.title: Who meets whom
transcript.text: So how do people mix? Not evenly. The same few people at home every day, groups at school and work, strangers now and then. Contact surveys show strong patterns by age. Children mostly meet children, working adults meet each other, and homes mix everyone. That's why closing schools and closing offices are different levers. They cut different parts of the contact network.

transcript.title: Uneven spread
transcript.text: People are uneven in another way, too. Some places, like a crowded indoor party, let one person infect many. We simulated two outbreaks with the same average, two new infections per case. In one, cases are all alike. In the other, very uneven. In the uneven one, three in four cases infect nobody, and just nine percent of cases cause eighty percent of all infections. And a single imported case dies out on its own eighty nine percent of the time, against twenty percent when cases are alike. So uneven spread makes outbreaks rarer, but more explosive when they take off. The average hides that.

transcript.title: Space, and what we see
transcript.text: Epidemics move through space as well. Commuters tie nearby towns together, and long trips seed outbreaks far away. In our two-town run, if two people in a thousand commute, the second town peaks twenty days after the first. At twenty in a thousand, nine days after. Then there's the gap between what happens and what we see. First infection, then symptoms, then a test, then a report. Every step adds delay. In our run, the reported curve peaks eight days after the real one, and shows only the thirty percent of infections that ever get tested. So the data is always a bit late and a bit partial. Remember that whenever someone shows you a case chart.

transcript.title: Kinds of germs
transcript.text: Now, one level deeper: biology. Germs come in several kinds: viruses, bacteria, fungi, single-celled parasites, worms, and misfolded proteins called prions. And being infected is not the same as being sick. Infection means the germ is in you, multiplying. Disease means symptoms. You can have the first without the second, and still pass it on.

transcript.title: Three clocks
transcript.text: Three clocks start at infection. The latent period ends when you become infectious. The incubation period ends when symptoms start. The infectious period is the window for spreading. Each clock varies from person to person, so think of them as distributions, not single numbers. What matters most is their order. In our toy numbers, R₀ is 2.5, and eight in ten sick people isolate. If almost all spread comes after symptoms, R drops to about 0.8. But if forty percent of spread happens before symptoms, the very same isolation only gets R down to about 1.4. Same effort, opposite outcomes. Timing inside the body becomes timing in policy.

transcript.title: Routes and defenses
transcript.text: To spread, a germ has to leave one body, survive the trip, and reach another in a big enough dose. The main routes are the air, touch, shared objects, water and food, blood or sex, and insects like mosquitoes. Each route points to its own defense. Air means ventilation and less crowding. Water means sanitation. Mosquitoes mean bed nets.

transcript.title: Immunity and spillover
transcript.text: Immunity is why epidemics slow down, and why they come back. It is not an on-off switch. It can block infection, cut spread, or soften the illness. And it can fade. In our run, when protection fades after about half a year, a second wave arrives around day two hundred forty. Smaller, but it comes back. And many pandemics begin with spillover, a germ jumping from animals to people. Human activity can lower each barrier along the way.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: spread is a tug of war, shaped by who meets whom, where, and how fast we notice. Biology sets the clocks, the routes and the immunity. Next time, the people: fear, trust and money. Because what people do moves an epidemic as much as the virus does.

episodes.title: Fear, trust and money
episodes.hook: Same virus, same city, and yet an epidemic can rise, plateau or come back in waves.
episodes.takeaway: Behavior is part of the epidemic: fear flattens the curve, fatigue brings it back, and money decides who can protect.

transcript.title: The difference is us
transcript.text: Same virus, same city, same season. And yet the epidemic can rise, plateau, or come back in waves. The difference is us. Today, the psychology and the economics of pandemics. Fear, trust and money.

transcript.title: The behavior loop
transcript.text: The core idea is a loop. Disease changes behavior, and behavior changes disease. When people see cases rising, many stay home, avoid crowds, wear masks, get tested. Transmission drops. Then cases fall, and people relax.

transcript.title: Perceived risk
transcript.text: But people don't react to the true risk. They react to the risk they perceive, and our minds take shortcuts. Vivid, recent, heavily covered events feel more likely than they are. Slow, quiet risks feel smaller, until they hit close to home. So two towns facing the same epidemic can behave very differently, depending on what they believe is happening.

transcript.title: From belief to action
transcript.text: Belief alone isn't enough, either. A classic model of behavior says intention comes from three things: your attitude, what you think others expect, and whether you feel able to do it. If masks feel useless, or staying home means losing your job, intention never turns into action. And we copy each other. A visible, normal habit spreads through offices and schools. When it becomes rare, or a badge of one side, people drop it.

transcript.title: Trust and misinformation
transcript.text: Trust sits in the middle. When people trust health authorities and local messengers, they follow advice, and accept it when advice changes. Being open about uncertainty is how that trust is built. And misinformation spreads like a pathogen of its own. A large study of Twitter found that false stories spread farther and faster than true ones, mostly because people share what feels new. So in a pandemic two things spread at once: the virus, and beliefs about the virus.

transcript.title: Fatigue: our behavior model
transcript.text: Then there's fatigue. The World Health Organization calls pandemic fatigue an expected response to long restrictions. Motivation wears down. We built a small model of all this. Protection cuts transmission, people react to cases reported a week late, and they remember them for about five weeks. With no reaction at all, thirty percent of the town is infected at once at the peak, and ninety four percent get infected overall. Add fear, and the peak drops below one percent. After a year and a half, only about nine percent have been infected. Now add fatigue, so protection slowly wears off. The first wave falls, then the curve climbs back into a second, bigger wave around month nine. Forty percent infected. Fear flattens the curve. Fatigue brings the wave back. You'll play with this exact model in the lab.

transcript.title: Work, externalities, sick pay
transcript.text: Now, money. Most infections happen during ordinary economic life: working, shopping, commuting, caring for others. Someone who can work from home cuts contacts and keeps their pay. Someone whose job is on site faces a hard choice between health and rent. Economists call the core problem an externality. If I go to work sick, I keep my pay, but my coworkers carry the risk. Sick pay changes the math. In our toy numbers, with R₀ of 2.5, if four in ten sick workers can afford to stay home, R is about two. If eight in ten can, it drops to about 1.4. And a study of the 2020 emergency sick leave law in the United States linked it to slower case growth.

transcript.title: Pulling back, shocks, inequality
transcript.text: People also pull back on their own. Early in COVID-19, visits to shops fell sharply, and studies found that official orders explained only part of the drop. So a pandemic hits supply and demand at once. Workers get sick or stay home with kids. Restaurants and travel collapse, while delivery and video calls boom. And one closed factory can stall many others down the supply chain. The costs aren't shared equally. Jobs that can't be done from home, little savings, crowded housing. Those groups carry more risk, and more loss.

transcript.title: Targeting and what counts
transcript.text: That unevenness can also be a tool. In our toy town, a fifth of people work in busy settings, with four times the contacts. Remove a quarter of all contacts across the board, and R goes from 2.5 to about 1.9. Remove the same quarter only in the busy settings, and R drops to about 1.3. Targeting isn't always easy or fair. But ignoring differences gives policies that cost more and work less. And deaths are only one outcome. Long illness, mental health, lost schooling and delayed care all count.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So behavior is part of the epidemic. Perception, norms, trust and fatigue move contacts up and down, and money decides who can actually protect themselves. Next time: governments, and the big loop that ties biology, people, money and policy together.

episodes.title: Governments and feedback loops
episodes.hook: No government can stop a virus by decree, but governments shape what it needs.
episodes.takeaway: Timing, packages and late data: governments shape what the virus needs, and models map futures, not one forecast.

transcript.title: What governments shape
transcript.text: No government can stop a virus by decree. But governments shape almost everything a virus needs: how often we meet, where, and how fast cases are found. Today, the last part of Module two: the role of government, and the loop that ties everything together.

transcript.title: A collective action problem
transcript.text: A pandemic is a collective action problem. Even when everyone knows what helps, it's hard to keep up without coordination, good information and practical support. So governments provide what individuals and markets can't: surveillance, lab networks, emergency logistics, clear rules, and shared resources like hospitals.

transcript.title: Built before the crisis
transcript.text: Much of it has to exist before the crisis. Legal authority to act, trained public health staff, labs that can test and sequence, data systems that share, and agencies that already know each other. Internationally, under the International Health Regulations, countries have agreed to build these capacities and to report unusual outbreaks quickly. And legitimacy matters. When people see the system as competent and fair, the same effect needs much less force. Trust is a variable that changes transmission.

transcript.title: During the crisis
transcript.text: Early in an outbreak, the first job is to reduce uncertainty fast: testing, case definitions, reporting pipelines, and data people can actually read. Once spread is sustained, the job becomes interruption: support for isolation, contact tracing, testing, cleaner indoor air, masks, limits on crowding, and protecting hospitals. And here's the catch. The effect depends on timing and adherence, not on the announcement.

transcript.title: Timing decides
transcript.text: We tested timing in our model. The same measure, halving transmission for sixty days, started on different days. Start on day twenty, and the wave just waits. When the measure lifts, it comes back, with about twenty three percent of the town infected at once. Start on day sixty, and the peak has already passed. Start on day forty, and the same sixty days cut the peak from thirty percent to about eighteen, and total infections from ninety four percent to seventy seven. Same measure, same length. The calendar decided the outcome.

transcript.title: Policies interact
transcript.text: Policies also interact. Testing only helps if people can isolate, and isolation needs support, like paid leave and food delivery. In our toy numbers, R₀ is 2.5. More testing alone brings R to about 2.1. Isolation support alone, about the same. Both together, about 1.5. So good governance is less about one perfect measure, and more about a package that fits together, and can actually be delivered.

transcript.title: Delivery, equity, supplies
transcript.text: Delivery is the hard part. Tests that people can't reach. Isolation advice without pay. Tracers overwhelmed. Beds without staff. The virus finds every gap. Equity is part of this. If the most exposed groups can't protect themselves, transmission stays high for everyone. And strong measures must be justified, proportionate and safeguarded. Then supplies: tests, protective gear, vaccines, cold chains, and fast but careful approvals. When cases double every three and a half days, one week of delay means four times as many cases. And pandemics cross borders, while governments answer first to their own people. That makes global sharing hardest exactly when it's needed most.

transcript.title: The loop, and late data
transcript.text: Now let's tie Module two together. Biology sets the clocks. Contacts turn biology into spread. Psychology changes contacts. Money decides who can change. Government coordinates, and sends signals. And government reacts to data that arrives late, after incubation, testing and reporting. Decisions always look a little into the past. In our model, restrictions switch on when infections pass one percent, and off below 0.3 percent. Acting on true numbers, the peak stays near two percent. Acting on data ten days late, the peak is about three times higher.

transcript.title: What models can honestly do
transcript.text: This coupling makes epidemics sensitive. Early on, exponential growth turns small timing gaps into big differences, and chance, like one superspreading event, can decide what happens next. It also makes modeling hard. Key quantities aren't observed directly, like true infections, or how many people really isolate. And different assumptions can fit the same data. Here are two of our runs, one with R₀ two, one with R₀ three. For the first month they're almost identical. Then one peaks at fifteen percent, the other at thirty. So the honest job of a model is not to predict one future. It's to map plausible futures, say what must be true for a policy to work, and show which unknowns matter.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: That's Module two. The virus is one part of a coupled system of biology, people, money and government. Next, in Module three, we start writing that system in mathematics, with compartmental models. See you there.

episodes.title: SIR from scratch and the meaning of R₀
episodes.hook: The workhorse of epidemic modeling, built from scratch: three boxes, five assumptions, two rates.
episodes.takeaway: SIR from scratch: R0 = β/γ, growth needs S > 1/R0, and the epidemic stops before everyone is infected.

transcript.title: Compartmental models
transcript.text: Welcome to Module three. For the next six episodes, we build the field's workhorse: compartmental models. We start with the simplest one, the SIR model. Three boxes, two arrows, and a surprising amount of insight.

transcript.title: Three boxes, five assumptions
transcript.text: Split the population into three groups. Susceptible people can catch it. Infected people can pass it on. Removed people are out of the game: recovered, isolated, or dead. The basic model makes five simplifying assumptions. Everyone mixes with everyone, equally. New infections follow mass action. And nobody is born, dies of other causes, or moves away. Recovery gives permanent immunity. And the time someone stays infectious is random, with the same chance of recovering every day. None of these is literally true. They give us a clean baseline, and every later model relaxes one of them.

transcript.title: The SIR equations
transcript.text: Now the equations. Susceptible people become infected at rate beta, times S, times I. Infected people recover at rate gamma, times I. Beta packs two things together: how often people meet, and the chance that a meeting passes the infection on. One over gamma is the average time someone stays infectious. One choice matters more than it looks. Written like this, transmission grows with the size of the crowd. Divide by the population, and each person makes a fixed number of contacts, however big the town is.

transcript.title: R0, the threshold and the peak
transcript.text: At the start, almost everyone is susceptible, so each case infects about beta over gamma people in total. That's the basic reproduction number, R₀. In our run, beta is 0.3 per day, and people stay infectious for ten days. So R₀ is three. Another way to see it: ten contacts a day, a three percent chance of passing it on per contact, for ten days. Ten times 0.03 times ten is three. And R₀ is not speed. Early on, infections grow at rate beta minus gamma, 0.2 per day here, so they double about every three and a half days. Two diseases with the same R₀ can grow at very different speeds. Infections grow only while the susceptible share is above one over R₀. Here, one third. As susceptibles run out, the effective number, R₀ times the susceptible share, falls. It crosses one exactly at the peak. In our run, around day thirty eight. So the peak isn't when the virus gets tired. It's when there aren't enough susceptible people left for each case to replace itself.

transcript.title: Final size and overshoot
transcript.text: Here's the second surprise. The epidemic ends while some people were never infected. Take time out of the equations and you get the final size relation. The total share infected depends only on R₀. An R₀ of 1.5 infects about fifty eight percent. Two, about eighty percent. Three, about ninety four percent. And notice the overshoot. With R₀ three, herd immunity is reached when two thirds are immune, but the epidemic runs on to ninety four percent, because so many people are still infected at that moment. That gap matters for policy. Vaccinating two thirds before an outbreak prevents it. Reaching two thirds immune by infection costs another quarter of the town on top.

transcript.title: Counts can't go negative
transcript.text: One sanity check before we build bigger models: counts can't go negative. In the exact equations, they never do. S can only shrink toward zero, R only grows, and I can never cross below zero. So if your simulation shows a negative number of susceptible people, the model isn't wrong. Your numerical method is. Take ten-day steps with the simplest method, and S drops below zero. More in Module twelve.

transcript.title: What we observe
transcript.text: And in real life, we never see S, I and R. We see reported cases, hospital admissions and deaths. So applied models add an observation layer on top: only a share of infections gets reported, with delays and noise. The SIR flows stay the same; the layer links them to the data. Modules seven and eight live there.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: three boxes, two rates. R₀ is beta over gamma, the threshold is a susceptible share of one over R₀, and the final size depends only on R₀. Next time, we add more boxes: births and deaths, reinfection, and a latent period.

episodes.title: More states: births, deaths, reinfection, latency
episodes.hook: The basic SIR model has one wave.
episodes.takeaway: Births refill susceptibles, fading immunity brings waves back, and latency changes the timing, not the total.

transcript.title: Real diseases come back
transcript.text: The basic SIR model has one wave, and then it's over forever. Real diseases come back. Today, three ways to bring them back, and one way to slow them down. We add births and deaths, reinfection, and a latent period.

transcript.title: Births, deaths, endemic waves
transcript.text: First, births and deaths. Babies arrive susceptible, and everyone dies of other causes at some rate. Now the susceptible pool keeps refilling, so the disease can settle in for good. That's an endemic disease. At balance, the susceptible share is exactly one over R₀. In our town, R₀ is five, so a fifth of people are susceptible at any time. It also tells us the average age at infection: roughly life expectancy divided by R₀ minus one. With a fifty-year life expectancy, about twelve and a half years. The higher R₀, the earlier in life people catch it. That's why measles, with a very high R₀, used to be a disease of childhood. Started near that balance, the disease comes back in waves every four to six years, each one a bit smaller, as it settles down. No seasons, no behavior change. The waves come from births alone, slowly refilling the pool. Near balance, theory predicts a period of about 3.7 years for these waves. Our run starts a bit away from balance, so its first waves are slower, and they speed up as they settle.

transcript.title: How much vaccination
transcript.text: This also tells us how much vaccination we need. Vaccinate a share of newborns, and R₀ effectively shrinks by that share. To eliminate the disease, push it below one. With R₀ five, that's eighty percent of newborns.

transcript.title: Reinfection: SIS and SIRS
transcript.text: Second, reinfection. If recovery gives no immunity at all, people go straight back to susceptible. That's the S I S model. With R₀ three, it settles at two thirds of people infected at any time. A steady state, with no waves. Some bacterial infections behave roughly like this, since recovering from them leaves little protection. If immunity lasts a while and then fades, that's S I R S. In our run, immunity lasts a year on average. After the big first wave, smaller waves follow about every nine months, and it settles near two percent infected. Common colds and seasonal coronaviruses are closer to this picture: you can catch the same virus again a year or two later.

transcript.title: Latency: SEIR
transcript.text: Third, latency. Newly infected people usually can't infect others right away. So we add an exposed box, E, between S and I. With the same R₀ of three and five days of latency, growth slows down a lot. Cases double every seven days, instead of every three and a half. The peak comes on day seventy four instead of day thirty eight, and it's lower: twenty percent infected at once, instead of thirty. But the final size is the same, ninety four percent. Latency changes the timing, not the total.

transcript.title: Erlang stages, and which box
transcript.text: One more refinement. In a single exposed box, people leave at a constant rate, so some leave after one day and some after twenty. Real latent periods are more regular. The trick is to split E into several stages in a row. Same average, much less spread. With four stages, the peak in our run moves from day seventy four to day eighty. Small, but it matters when you fit real data. So which box do you add? It depends on the disease and the question. Births and deaths for long time scales, waning for diseases you can catch again, latency whenever the delay to infectiousness matters for timing or control.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: births refill the susceptible pool and make a disease endemic. Fading immunity brings waves back. Latency stretches the timeline without changing the total. Next time, more classes: different kinds of infected people, hospital outcomes, age groups, and mosquitoes.

episodes.title: More classes: stages, outcomes, structure, vectors
episodes.hook: Not every infected person is the same.
episodes.takeaway: Stages, outcomes, groups and vectors: hidden stages sustain spread, hospitals lag, and bites count twice.

transcript.title: Not every infection is the same
transcript.text: Not every infected person is the same. Some never feel sick, some spread it before they know it, and some end up in hospital. Today, we give each of them a box.

transcript.title: Several infectious stages
transcript.text: Picture a toy disease. Everyone spends two days infectious before symptoms. Then seven in ten get sick for five days, and three in ten never show symptoms and spread at half the rate. Add up the contribution of each stage, and R₀ comes out at about 1.9. About a third of that comes before symptoms, more than half from people with symptoms, and twelve percent from people who never feel ill. Now suppose people with symptoms isolate after one day. R₀ drops to about 1.04. Much better, but still above one. The hidden stages keep it going. The structure of the infected classes decides what control can achieve.

transcript.title: Hospital, deaths and delays
transcript.text: Next, outcomes. Instead of one removed box, we track who goes to hospital, and who dies. In our run, three percent of infections need a hospital bed for ten days, and half a percent are fatal, about three weeks after infection. New infections peak on day eighty six. Hospital occupancy peaks on day one hundred four, at about five hundred fifty beds per hundred thousand people. Deaths peak on day one hundred six. A word on two ratios. The infection fatality ratio divides deaths by all infections. The case fatality ratio divides deaths by reported cases. Early in an outbreak, when few mild cases are tested, the second can be many times the first. That lag is the point. By the time hospitals are fullest, new infections have been falling for almost three weeks.

transcript.title: Structured populations
transcript.text: Third, structure. People differ by age, risk or place, and they mix unevenly, as we saw in Module two. So we split the population into groups, each with its own S, I and R, linked by a contact matrix. In our two-group town, a quarter of people are children, and they have many more contacts. Ninety five percent of children get infected, against seventy three percent of adults. With more groups, say ten age bands, we get ten copies of the equations, and a ten by ten matrix of who infects whom. Bigger, but the same idea. One R₀ for the whole town hides that. The last episode of this module shows how to get one honest number out of a matrix like this.

transcript.title: Vectors: mosquitoes
transcript.text: Last, vectors. Malaria and dengue need a mosquito in between. People infect mosquitoes, and mosquitoes infect people. So we couple two models: S I R for people, and S I for mosquitoes, which usually stay infected for the rest of their short lives. Mosquitoes add their own clock too. After biting an infected person, the parasite needs days to develop inside the mosquito, and many mosquitoes die before it's ready. Toy numbers: one infected person infects ten mosquitoes, and each infected mosquito infects 0.3 people. From person to person, over the two steps, that's three. Halve the number of mosquitoes, and it drops to 1.5. But halve the bites, with bed nets, and it drops to 0.75. Below one. Bites count twice: a mosquito bites to get infected, and bites again to pass it on. That's why the biting rate appears squared in the classic Ross Macdonald formula.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: split the infected by stage, track outcomes with their delays, split the population into groups, and couple hosts with vectors. Next time, we let the rates change over time: seasons, interventions and behavior.

episodes.title: When transmission changes
episodes.hook: Transmission is never constant.
episodes.takeaway: β moves: seasons as a yearly wave, interventions as steps, behavior as feedback; R(t) is not R0.

transcript.title: Beta is never constant
transcript.text: So far, beta has been a constant. In real life, it never is. Winter comes, schools close, people get scared. Today, beta becomes a function of time.

transcript.title: Seasons
transcript.text: Start with seasons. Many respiratory infections spread better in winter: people crowd indoors, and some viruses survive longer in cold, dry air. Schools add their own rhythm. Classic studies of measles found that epidemics followed the school calendar: transmission rose when terms started, and fell during holidays. A simple model: beta goes up and down once a year, twenty percent above and below its average. From peak to trough, that's a ratio of 1.5. Combine that with immunity that fades after about a year. Without seasons, our model settles at a steady 1.6 percent infected. With seasons, it locks into a yearly wave, peaking at about eight percent, right around the time transmission is highest. A modest swing in beta becomes a big swing in cases, because the epidemic amplifies it. And the timing of the yearly peak is set by the season, not by when the first case arrived. In our run, the first wave peaks on day thirty nine; a few years later, every peak lands within a day of the yearly high point of transmission.

transcript.title: Interventions as steps
transcript.text: Next, interventions. The simplest way is piecewise: beta drops on the day a measure starts, and comes back on the day it ends. In reality, measures switch on gradually, and not everyone complies. A smoother ramp, or a compliance share, can capture that. But steps are a good first sketch. In our run, a measure cuts transmission from day thirty to day ninety. A twenty percent cut lowers the peak from thirty percent to twenty two. A forty percent cut brings it down to thirteen. But a sixty percent cut does worse than forty: the peak is fifteen percent, on day one hundred fifteen. Strong but short, and most people are still susceptible when it ends. More is not always better, if it stops too soon. Strength and timing work together. This is the same lesson as in Module two, now written as a beta that changes on chosen days. We'll optimize those days properly in Module ten.

transcript.title: Feedback and the product form
transcript.text: Third, beta can depend on the epidemic itself. When cases rise, people cut contacts, and beta falls. We built exactly this in Module two. Then beta is no longer a function of time alone. It depends on the state of the system, and that feedback can create plateaus and new waves. A handy way to write all of this: beta of t equals a baseline, times a season factor, times a policy factor, times a behavior factor. Each factor is a small model of its own.

transcript.title: R0 versus R(t)
transcript.text: One warning about words. R₀ is defined at the start, with everyone susceptible and nothing changed. Once beta changes, what you measure is the effective reproduction number, R t. It includes immunity, interventions, behavior and season, all at once. Estimating R t from data is a big topic of its own: you need the delays from infection to report, and the typical gap between one infection and the next. We'll see the tools in Module seven. So when the news says R is now 0.9, it means R t, not R₀.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: seasons as a smooth yearly wave, interventions as steps, and behavior as feedback. Same model, with a beta that moves. Next time, we stop pretending that everything is smooth and certain. Chance.

episodes.title: Chance matters: stochastic models
episodes.hook: In the equations, one case always starts an epidemic if R0 is above one.
episodes.takeaway: Chance decides whether an outbreak takes off (about 1/R0 fizzle); the equations describe it if it does.

transcript.title: One case: fizzle or take off
transcript.text: In the equations, one infected person in a town of a thousand always starts an epidemic, if R₀ is above one. In reality, the first case often just recovers, and that's the end of it.

transcript.title: Random events, Gillespie
transcript.text: To capture that, we switch from smooth flows to random events. People are whole numbers. Either someone gets infected, or someone recovers. Each event has a rate: beta times S times I over N for an infection, gamma times I for a recovery. The time to the next event is random, and so is which event it is. Simulating this one event at a time is called the Gillespie algorithm. Run it many times, and you get a whole distribution of outbreaks, instead of one curve. There are faster cousins, too. Tau-leaping jumps ahead by small time steps and draws how many events happened. Chain binomial models, like the classic Reed Frost model, move in whole generations.

transcript.title: Early extinction and 1/R0
transcript.text: We ran it two thousand times in a town of a thousand, starting from one case, with R₀ of two. In forty nine percent of the runs, the outbreak died out on its own after a handful of cases. The rest took off. Theory predicts this. Early on, the outbreak is a branching process, and with these assumptions the chance of extinction is one over R₀. One half. With R₀ three, we got thirty two percent, against a third in theory. And starting from three cases instead of one, the chance drops to about one in eight.

transcript.title: Tiny or big outbreaks
transcript.text: So the outcomes split in two. Either a tiny outbreak, or a big one. Almost nothing in between. And when it takes off, the big outbreak matches the smooth model closely: about eighty percent infected on average, just like the equations. The equations describe what happens if it takes off. Chance decides whether it takes off.

transcript.title: Timing spread and bands
transcript.text: Timing varies too. Among the big outbreaks with R₀ two, the peak came on day sixty six on average, give or take fifteen days. That matters for planning. A single smooth curve hides that spread. Instead of one curve, report a band: the range where, say, ninety percent of the simulated epidemics fall. That band is an honest picture of chance alone, before we even question the parameters.

transcript.title: When chance matters
transcript.text: So when do you need a stochastic model? When numbers are small: the first cases, a small community, the tail end of an epidemic, or elimination. Small numbers also cause fade-out. After a big wave, cases can drop so low that the chain breaks by chance. For measles, studies found it kept circulating without fade-out only in cities of a few hundred thousand people or more. That's the critical community size. When numbers are large, the smooth equations give a good average, and they're much cheaper to run. And remember Module two: if spread is uneven, early extinction gets even more likely, and the outbreaks that survive are more explosive. This randomness comes from individual events, so it shrinks as the population grows. A different kind, like a random cold spell, hits everyone at once, and doesn't average out.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: random events, many runs, a distribution. Early extinction with a chance of about one over R₀, and big outbreaks that look like the equations. Next time, the last tool of this module: the next generation matrix, for when one simple R₀ formula is not enough.

episodes.title: The next-generation matrix
episodes.hook: When one formula for R0 is not enough: the next-generation matrix.
episodes.takeaway: The next-generation matrix: R0 is its dominant eigenvalue, and it shows where transmission lives.

transcript.title: When beta over gamma breaks
transcript.text: R₀ equals beta over gamma works for one simple model. Add stages, age groups or mosquitoes, and that formula breaks. Today, the general recipe.

transcript.title: Generations and the matrix
transcript.text: The idea is to follow infections from generation to generation. For a typical infected person of each type, ask: how many new infected people of each type do they cause? Put those numbers in a matrix, called the next generation matrix. R₀ is its dominant eigenvalue: the long-run growth factor per generation, once the mix of infected types settles down.

transcript.title: F and V, and SEIR
transcript.text: To build it, split the equations of the infected boxes in two. F holds new infections arriving. V holds everything else: moves between infected boxes, and exits. The matrix is F times the inverse of V. In words: new infections per day, times the time spent in each infected box. Try it on S E I R. Only I creates new infections, and the latent box just delays things. The recipe gives R₀ equal to beta over gamma, the same as S I R. Latency cancels out. In symbols: F has beta in the corner, V has sigma and gamma, and the product gives sigma over sigma, times beta over gamma. The sigma, the latent rate, cancels.

transcript.title: The two-group town
transcript.text: Now our two-group town from two episodes ago. Children are a quarter of the town, but they meet each other a lot. One infected child infects about 2.1 children and 1.3 adults. One infected adult infects about 0.4 children and 1.3 adults. Neither group alone tells the story. Children alone would give 2.1, adults alone 1.3. The dominant eigenvalue of the matrix is about 2.5. And its eigenvector tells us who the cases are, generation after generation: about half children and half adults, though children are only a quarter of the town. The same recipe handles Episode three's toy disease: presymptomatic, symptomatic and asymptomatic stages are three infected boxes, and the matrix adds up their contributions to 1.9, as before.

transcript.title: Comparing policies
transcript.text: Now we can compare policies properly. Cut contacts among children by sixty percent, say by closing schools, and R₀ falls from 2.5 to 1.8. Cut contacts among adults by the same sixty percent, and it only falls to 2.4. Same cut, very different effect. The matrix shows where transmission really lives. You can push this further: ask how much R₀ changes when you change each entry of the matrix. Those sensitivities point to the transmission routes worth targeting first.

transcript.title: Vectors and conventions
transcript.text: One subtlety with vectors. In the next generation matrix, one generation is one step: person to mosquito, or mosquito to person. So for our mosquito toy, the matrix gives the square root of three, about 1.7, instead of three over two steps. Same threshold at one, different number. Always check which one a paper uses.

transcript.title: The fine print
transcript.text: And the fine print. The recipe describes the start of an outbreak, near a disease-free state. It doesn't give you the peak or the final size. And how you split F and V is a modeling choice. Different splits can give different numbers, with the same threshold at one.

transcript.title: Module 3 recap
transcript.text: That's Module three: SIR and its family, rates that change over time, chance, and a recipe for R₀ that works for any number of infected types. Next, Module four: space. Cities linked by travel, networks of people, and epidemics that move like waves across a map.

episodes.title: Cities linked by travel
episodes.hook: Space enters the model: cities linked by travel.
episodes.takeaway: Travel decides when an epidemic arrives, not how big it gets; arrival follows effective distance, not the map.

transcript.title: When will it arrive?
transcript.text: An outbreak starts in one city. When does it reach the next city, and the one after that? Today, space enters the model, starting with cities linked by travel. And here's where we're heading: travel decides when an epidemic arrives far more than the map does.

transcript.title: Patches linked by travel
transcript.text: Split the map into patches: cities, districts, regions. Inside each patch, people mix well, so each patch runs its own S I R. Patches are linked by movement. A matrix M holds the travel rates: m p q is the share of patch p's people who travel to patch q each day. Travelers carry their state with them. A susceptible traveler arrives susceptible. An infected one arrives infected, and seeds the next city. This is the flux, or migration, form. People really relocate, and every compartment flows along the links. The total population stays the same; only where people are changes.

transcript.title: Moving people or moving risk
transcript.text: There's a second way to link patches. Most travel is commuting: people visit another city during the day and come home at night. Then we keep everyone at home and let infection pressure travel instead. The force of infection in patch p adds up contact with infected people from every patch, weighted by how much the two patches mix. Moving people, or moving risk. Pick the one that matches your data: migration records, or commuting and visit data.

transcript.title: Two clocks: growth and travel
transcript.text: Let's see what travel does. Five cities in a row, each with R₀ of three, each linked only to its neighbors. The first city has the outbreak. With very little travel, three people in ten thousand a day, the waves come one after another. The last city peaks on day one hundred thirty seven, eighty seven days after the first. With a lot of travel, one person in ten a day, all five cities peak within two days of each other, around day fifty eight. And either way, every city ends with about ninety four percent infected. Travel changes the timing, not the total. Two clocks are racing: how fast the epidemic grows inside a city, and how fast people move between cities. Weak travel gives a chain of local epidemics. Strong travel merges them into one.

transcript.title: Effective distance
transcript.text: Now a more realistic map: eight cities of different sizes. Travel falls off with distance, plus one air link between the two big cities. The outbreak starts in the big city on the left. Its nearest neighbor is reached on day twenty four. The other big city, near the far end, across the air link: day ten. Distance on the map explains almost none of the arrival times. R squared is 0.05. So measure distance by travel instead. Brockmann and Helbing defined an effective distance: one minus the log of the share of travelers going from one city to the next, added up along the best route. With effective distance, arrival times fall on a straight line: R squared of 0.99. The epidemic moves like a wave, in travel space, not on the map.

transcript.title: Imported sparks
transcript.text: Travel can also keep an outbreak going where it would die out alone. Take a small town where each case infects only 0.8 others. On its own, a few cases fizzle: less than half a percent of the town is ever infected. Now let one tenth of the town's contacts be with visitors from a big city, where R₀ is two. The town ends with thirty six percent infected. Locally, R₀ is below one, yet the town is hit hard, because sparks keep arriving. So don't only ask if R₀ is above one. Ask how often sparks arrive.

transcript.title: R0 of a network of patches
transcript.text: So what is R₀ for a whole network of patches? The next generation matrix from Module three answers it: the local reproduction numbers, combined through the mixing matrix. R₀ is its dominant eigenvalue. Take one hot city where each case infects 1.6 people, and four cool cities at 0.8. On its own, the hot city sustains an outbreak. Mix them, and the hot city's cases spend part of their contacts in cool cities. Mix half of all contacts, and R₀ falls to 1.1. Mix three quarters, and it reaches one. Now flip it. Five cities just below one, at 0.95. Turn one into a hotspot at 1.6, with thirty percent mixing, and the whole network goes above one, to 1.27. One hotspot can carry a region.

transcript.title: Border closures
transcript.text: Real models add more: different parameters per city, so some cities export infection and others import it; commuting that differs on weekdays and weekends; and travel that changes over time. Like a border closure. Two cities linked by travel. Cut the travel to one twentieth on day seven, and the second city's outbreak arrives four days later, and peaks a week later. Cut it on day zero, and the peak comes two weeks later. Cut it on day twenty, after the virus has arrived, and it buys three days. And every time, the second city still ends with ninety four percent infected. A closure buys time: to prepare, to treat, to vaccinate. It doesn't buy immunity.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: patches with their own S I R, linked by travel. Weak links give a chain of waves; strong links synchronize them. Arrival follows effective distance, and imported sparks can keep places burning that couldn't burn on their own. Next time, we zoom in from cities to people: epidemics on networks of contacts.

episodes.title: Networks of people
episodes.hook: Same average contacts, very different epidemics.
episodes.takeaway: On networks the threshold depends on excess degree: hubs lower it and speed spread, clustering slows it.

transcript.title: Same contacts, different epidemics
transcript.text: Two towns. In both, people have four contacts on average. In one, the epidemic peaks after about a hundred days. In the other, in under a month. The difference is who is connected to whom.

transcript.title: Contact networks and T
transcript.text: In a contact network, people are nodes, and an edge is a chance to infect: a household, the person at the next desk, a weekly meeting. Infection moves along edges. An infected person infects each susceptible neighbor at a rate, tau, and recovers at rate gamma. So every edge has a transmissibility, T: the chance it transmits before the infected end recovers. T equals tau over tau plus gamma. In our runs, one third.

transcript.title: The percolation picture
transcript.text: Now a beautiful shortcut. Flip a weighted coin for every edge: with probability T, it would transmit if it got the chance. Keep those edges, and delete the rest. A large outbreak is possible only if the kept edges form one giant connected cluster. That links epidemics to percolation, a classic problem in physics. For final sizes on random networks, the percolation picture is close to exact. It says nothing about timing, so for peaks and speed we still simulate.

transcript.title: Excess degree and the threshold
transcript.text: When does the giant cluster appear? When T, times the mean excess degree, is above one. Excess degree is how many other contacts a person has when you reach them by following an edge. And following edges is exactly what an infection does. The catch: edges lead to well-connected people more often. In our hub-heavy network, people have about four contacts on average, but the person at the end of a random edge has more than eleven. Your friends have more friends than you do. So the threshold drops. A random network with four contacts on average needs T above a quarter. The hub-heavy one, with the same average, needs T above about one in ten. With T of one third, both can take off. But the hub network peaks around day twenty seven, against day one hundred five for the random one, and infects half the town instead of forty four percent.

transcript.title: Hubs first
transcript.text: Look at who gets infected over time. In the first week, new cases on the hub network have about ten contacts each. By the tenth week, fewer than four. Hubs are infected early, and they spread fast. Then the epidemic runs out of hubs and slows down. That's one reason early growth can fool a forecast.

transcript.title: Clustering
transcript.text: Now clustering. In real life, your friends often know each other. That makes triangles. Triangles waste transmissions. By the time you could infect your friend's friend, your friend may already have done it. Compare two networks where everyone has exactly four contacts. One is wired at random. In the other, neighbors share friends. With T of one half, the random one takes off in sixty nine percent of runs, and infects eighty five percent of the town. The clustered one takes off in only thirteen percent of runs, and even then infects about twelve percent. Same number of contacts. A very different epidemic.

transcript.title: Diseases you can catch again
transcript.text: For diseases you can catch again, like S I S, the question is whether infection keeps circulating. There, a common approximation makes the threshold spectral: tau over gamma has to beat one over the largest eigenvalue of the network's adjacency matrix. That eigenvalue is driven by dense cores. For our hub network it's about thirteen, for the random one about five. A tight core keeps reinfecting itself.

transcript.title: Interventions on the graph
transcript.text: Networks make interventions concrete. Vaccination removes nodes. Distancing removes edges. Contact tracing follows the edges of each case. On the hub network, with T of one half, almost half the town is infected without vaccination. Vaccinate twenty percent of people at random, and it's still twenty seven percent. Vaccinate the best-connected twenty percent, and the epidemic is gone: under one in a thousand. But that needs the whole contact network, which nobody has. A clever trick works without it. Pick random people, and vaccinate one of their friends. Friends tend to be hubs. Cohen and colleagues called it acquaintance immunization. With twenty percent, the attack rate falls under four percent.

transcript.title: Middle paths and when to use networks
transcript.text: Between simulating every person and assuming everyone mixes, there are middle paths: tracking people by their number of contacts, or equations that follow whether each edge has transmitted yet. Use networks when contact structure matters: superspreading, households, targeted interventions. They're harder when the network is unknown or the population is huge. Often, a hybrid works: networks inside patches, and travel between them.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: edge transmissibility T, a threshold set by excess degree, hubs infected first, clustering that slows spread, and interventions as surgery on the graph. Next time, we go continuous: epidemics as waves moving across a map.

episodes.title: Epidemics in continuous space
episodes.hook: An epidemic as a wave crossing a map.
episodes.takeaway: Reaction plus diffusion makes waves with speed 2√(D r); borders, drift and long jumps reshape them.

transcript.title: A wave you can calculate
transcript.text: Drop ink in water, and it spreads out. Now let the ink multiply as it spreads. That's an epidemic wave crossing a map, and it moves at a speed you can calculate.

transcript.title: Densities, reaction and diffusion
transcript.text: Instead of patches, treat space as continuous. S, I and R become densities: how many susceptible, infected and recovered people live around each point. Every point runs the usual S I R. That's the reaction part. People also move. If each person takes many small random steps, then from far away the crowd spreads out smoothly. That's diffusion. The diffusion coefficient D grows with the square of the step length, divided by the time per step. Reaction plus diffusion: local infection, plus local movement. A reaction diffusion model.

transcript.title: A ring of infection
transcript.text: Here it is in a square town with closed borders, starting from one small seed. Infection grows where it is, and leaks into the neighborhood. The result is a ring of infection moving outward, with recovered people behind it, and susceptible people ahead.

transcript.title: The speed of the front
transcript.text: How fast does the front move? A classic result by Fisher, and by Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov, says: two times the square root of D times r. Here r is the early growth rate, beta minus gamma. Movement and growth set the speed together. In our runs, D is one square kilometer per day and r is 0.2. Theory says 0.89 kilometers a day. We measured 0.87. Multiply D by four, and the speed doubles: we measured 1.75, against 1.79 in theory. Movement matters, but through a square root. The measured fronts lag a little behind theory, because a front takes a long time to settle into its final speed.

transcript.title: Borders are assumptions
transcript.text: In continuous space, the edges of the map matter. A boundary condition is an epidemiological assumption.
