A closed border keeps everyone in: after a hundred fifty days, all of our diffusing crowd is still inside. An absorbing border removes whoever reaches it: forty percent left. A leaky border lets some through: almost sixty percent left. And a border held at a fixed level of infection acts like a constant source, seeding the region again and again. Fit a model with the wrong border, and you'll blame transmission for what was really travel.

transcript.title: Drift along corridors
transcript.text: Movement isn't always random. Commuters flow along corridors. Add a drift, a steady push in one direction, and the wave becomes lopsided. With a drift of 0.4 kilometers a day, the front moves downstream at 1.31, and upstream at only 0.51. Close to theory: the speed, plus or minus the drift.

transcript.title: Uneven landscapes
transcript.text: Landscapes are uneven too. Put in a strip where transmission is too low to sustain spread, like a thinly populated area. A five kilometer strip delays the wave by ten days. A forty kilometer strip, by eighty two days. But in these equations, the strip never stops the wave, because fractions of a person can cross it. With whole people, a wide enough gap can break the chain. The equations can't tell a millionth of a person from zero.

transcript.title: Long jumps
transcript.text: The biggest limit of diffusion: it only allows small steps. Real people also take planes. So replace diffusion with a kernel: how strongly an infected person affects people at each distance. A thin-tailed kernel behaves like diffusion: a steady front, about three quarters of a kilometer a day. A fat-tailed kernel, with rare long jumps, is a different story. New outbreaks pop up far ahead, and the front speeds up: one hundred sixty kilometers by day one hundred, and over a thousand by day one hundred forty. With long jumps, there's no single speed. Arrival is ruled by the rare long trips.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: reaction plus diffusion makes waves, with speed two root D r. Borders, drifts and uneven landscapes reshape them, and long jumps break the wave picture. Real models often combine both: smooth local spread, plus travel between hubs. Next time, the last episode of this module: bounding the spread with norms, to know if an outbreak will grow without solving everything.

episodes.title: Bounding the spread
episodes.hook: Will a 100-district outbreak grow or die out? The spectral radius decides; matrix norms bound it cheaply.
episodes.takeaway: Any matrix norm below one proves an outbreak dies out; the spectral radius tells the long run, norms the short run.

transcript.title: Will it grow?
transcript.text: A model with a hundred districts. Will the outbreak grow, or die out? You can't eyeball a hundred curves. Today: one number decides it, and cheaper numbers can bound it.

transcript.title: One generation at a time
transcript.text: Start near the beginning of an outbreak, when almost everyone is susceptible. Then new cases in each district depend linearly on the cases in all districts. Write the cases per district as a vector x. One generation later, x becomes A times x. Column q of A says what one case in district q causes, district by district. Growth or decay is set by the spectral radius of A: its largest eigenvalue, in size. Above one, the outbreak grows. Below one, it dies out. It's the next generation matrix again, now in space.

transcript.title: Norms: cheap sizes
transcript.text: But eigenvalues of big matrices can be costly, and often the matrix is only partly known. Norms are cheaper. A norm measures the size of a vector. The one norm is the total number of cases. The infinity norm is the worst district. A matrix norm measures how much a matrix can amplify, at most. The one norm of A is its largest column sum: the most cases that any single case can cause. The infinity norm is its largest row sum: the most pressure any one district can receive.

transcript.title: The guarantee
transcript.text: And here's the key fact: the spectral radius is never bigger than any of these norms. So if any one of them is below one, the outbreak must die out. Guaranteed. Our example: five districts. The largest column sum is 0.95. Every case causes fewer than one case. Decay is proven, without computing a single eigenvalue. The largest row sum is 1.1, so that norm can't decide. The true spectral radius is 0.92. A norm gives a guarantee in one direction only. Starting from a hundred cases, the total falls to about fifty within ten generations.

transcript.title: Short run, long run
transcript.text: Now the twist. The spectral radius tells you the long run. It doesn't tell you what happens first. Take six districts along a travel route. Each case causes half a case at home, and one case in the next district down the line. The spectral radius is one half, so it will die out. But the largest column sum is 1.5. And from a hundred cases, the total climbs to about thirteen hundred sixty by generation eight, before it falls. Both numbers are right. The norm bounds how fast cases can grow in each step. The eigenvalue tells you where it ends. Check only the eigenvalue, and a big transient wave can surprise you. Take the norm of A to the power k, then its k-th root. As k grows, it slowly approaches the spectral radius. That's Gelfand's formula: norms are the short-run view, the eigenvalue is the long run.

transcript.title: Keep and export
transcript.text: Norms also give simple policy rules. Say each case causes a share a at home, and a share b elsewhere, spread over the other districts by travel. Then every column sums to a plus b, and that sum is exactly the spectral radius. Keep 0.7 at home and export 0.2: that's 0.9, and the outbreak decays. Export 0.35 instead: 1.05, and it grows. So you can trade: cut local transmission, or cut exports. What counts is the sum.

transcript.title: Norms in continuous space
transcript.text: Norms work in continuous space too. Measure the infected density with an L two norm. With closed borders, diffusion only smooths. It can never make that norm grow faster than the local growth rate r. In our run, r was 0.2, and the fastest growth we saw was 0.17. With absorbing borders, diffusion even helps, because people carry infection out of the region. A strip of land with absorbing edges sustains an outbreak only if it's wider than a critical size: pi times the square root of D over r. For our numbers, about seven kilometers. At eighty percent of that width, the outbreak shrinks by about eleven percent a day. At a hundred twenty percent, it grows by six percent a day. Just as theory says.

transcript.title: From space to a graph
transcript.text: Finally, going from continuous space back to a graph. Split the map into regions, add up the people in each, and turn flows across borders into travel rates. Fewer regions make a cheaper model, but there's a price. On a line of a hundred twenty kilometers, the wave reaches the far third on day one hundred forty. A graph with three towns gets there on day seventy five. Far too early. Twelve towns: day one hundred fourteen. Forty eight towns: day one hundred thirty six. Each town mixes instantly inside, so coarse graphs make waves too fast. Choose regions small enough that people inside really do mix fast, compared with how fast the epidemic grows.

transcript.title: Module 4 recap
transcript.text: That's Module four: patches linked by travel, networks of people, waves in continuous space, and norms that bound them all. Next, Module five: when the pathogen itself changes. Several strains, immunity, and mutation.

episodes.title: Strains side by side
episodes.hook: Two strains, one pool of people.
episodes.takeaway: Strains compete for people: identical strains are labels, a fitter strain must arrive in time, and log odds reveal the advantage.

transcript.title: One virus, several strains
transcript.text: Flu comes in several strains every winter. COVID came in variant after variant. Today our model gets more than one strain, and we ask: when does one strain push out another?

transcript.title: A shared pool of susceptibles
transcript.text: Start with the simplest version. Each strain gets its own infected box and its own rates. But all strains draw from the same pool of susceptible people. And we make a strong assumption: recover from any strain, and you're immune to all of them. One shared recovered box. So strains never meet directly. They compete for people. Every person one strain infects is a person the other strain can no longer reach. Each strain's effective reproduction number is its own R₀ times the share still susceptible. When one strain uses up susceptibles, it pulls down the other strain's number too.

transcript.title: Identical strains
transcript.text: In the model, a strain is just a label we attach to infections. So here's a first test: several identical strains, each with R₀ of two, starting together from the same total number of cases. One strain, two, three or four: the epidemic is exactly the same every time. Eighty percent infected, with the peak on day sixty eight. Splitting an epidemic into labels doesn't make it bigger. The strains share it.

transcript.title: Timing beats fitness
transcript.text: Now make them different. Strain A has R₀ of 1.8. Strain B is fitter, with 2.6. If both start on day zero, B wins. It causes about sixty percent of all infections, and the epidemic reaches eighty six percent of the town, against seventy three percent with A alone. But let B arrive twenty days late, as a handful of cases, and it causes only fifteen percent of infections. Forty days late: one percent. Later than that: almost nothing. B is just as fit as before. Its R₀ never changed. It simply arrived after A had used up the people it needed. In a race for susceptibles, timing can beat fitness. Even on day sixty, B's effective reproduction number is still above two. But it starts from so few cases that A's wave is over before B can grow.

transcript.title: Reading a variant's advantage
transcript.text: There's a neat way to spot a fitter strain early: follow its share among new cases. While both strains are growing and B is still rare, the log odds of B's share rise in a straight line. The slope is the difference between the two transmission rates. Here, 0.08 per day, and that's exactly the slope in our run. That's how a variant's advantage is often read from data: plot the log odds of its share, and read the slope. In our run, B passed half of all cases on day fifty eight. Case counts alone can't show this. You need to know which strain each case has, and that means sequencing a sample of cases, which we'll meet in Module nine.

transcript.title: Beyond full protection
transcript.text: Real multi-strain models relax the strong assumption. Recovering from one strain rarely protects fully against another. Strains can also differ in latent period and severity, so each one may get its own exposed box. But the shared pool stays the core idea. Strains interact through the people they infect.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: parallel strains drawing from one pool of susceptibles. Identical strains don't add up to a bigger epidemic. A fitter strain wins only if it arrives in time. And the slope of the log odds of its share reveals its advantage. Next time: immunity that depends on your history. Who has had which strain, and what that does to the next wave.

episodes.title: Reinfection and immune history
episodes.hook: Who has had which strain? We track immune history, see how fast the number of boxes explodes, add cross-immunity, find the level above which a new strain can't take off, and follow four strains arriving every 150 days into wave after wave and repeat infections.
episodes.takeaway: Immune history decides who a new strain can reach: above a cross-immunity threshold it can't take off.

transcript.title: Protected against a new strain?
transcript.text: You had flu last winter. This winter, a different strain arrives. Are you protected? Partly. Today: immunity that depends on your history.

transcript.title: Immune histories
transcript.text: To model reinfection, we keep track of history: which strains each person has already had. With two strains, A and B, there are four histories: none, A only, B only, and both. People who had A can still catch B, and the other way round. Each strain gets an infected box for every history that hasn't had that strain yet. With two strains, that's four infected boxes. And it explodes. Four strains: sixteen histories and thirty two infected boxes. Ten strains: over a thousand histories, and five thousand one hundred twenty infected boxes. Compare a parallel model with ten strains and no history: just twelve boxes. Tracking history is more honest, and much more expensive.

transcript.title: Cross-immunity
transcript.text: History can change three things: how likely you are to be infected again, how sick you get, and how infectious you are. We'll focus on the first: cross-immunity. Say an earlier infection lowers your chance of catching a different strain by a share, sigma. Sigma of zero means no protection. Sigma of one means full protection, as in the last episode.

transcript.title: A second strain arrives
transcript.text: Our test: strain A, with R₀ of two and a half, sweeps through the town. By day one hundred fifty, eighty nine percent have had it. Then strain B arrives, just as transmissible. With no cross-immunity, B infects eighty nine percent all over again, in a second wave as high as the first. With sigma of one half, B still infects forty seven percent, in a lower and slower wave. With sixty percent protection, B creeps along for more than a year and infects twenty three percent. Above about two thirds, B can't take off at all. The tipping point is where B's effective reproduction number crosses one.

transcript.title: The invasion threshold
transcript.text: That number is B's R₀, times B's effective susceptible pool: everyone who never had B, weighted by how well protected they are. Here, that's the eleven percent never infected, plus the eighty nine percent who had A, counted at one minus sigma. Multiply by two and a half, set it equal to one, and sigma comes out at 0.67. So a strain's real potential depends on the immunity landscape it lands in, not just on its own R₀.

transcript.title: Waves of strains
transcript.text: Now four strains, arriving every hundred fifty days, each with R₀ of 2.4 and forty percent cross-immunity. We get wave after wave: twenty two percent infected at the first peak, then seven, six and five percent. Each new strain finds people its predecessors left only partly protected. By day eight hundred, more than half the town has been infected three or four times. Only one person in five hundred has never been infected. Immune history turns one epidemic into a sequence of waves. It's one of the ingredients behind repeated flu seasons and variant waves.

transcript.title: Shortcuts
transcript.text: Because full histories explode, modelers use shortcuts. They group histories into a few immune statuses, or place strains on a map of antigenic distance, where nearby strains protect more against each other. And one number per strain often summarizes it all: the effective susceptible share. Who could still catch this particular strain, and how easily.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: track immune history. Cross-immunity decides whether a new strain can invade. The threshold is its effective reproduction number in the landscape it lands in. And a sequence of strains makes a sequence of waves. Next time: where new strains come from. Mutation, during the epidemic itself.

episodes.title: Mutation and new strains
episodes.hook: New strains made during the epidemic.
episodes.takeaway: Mutation makes new strains; most new mutants fizzle, and fewer infections mean fewer chances to evolve.

transcript.title: Strains made during spread
transcript.text: So far, every strain was there from the start, or arrived from somewhere else. But new strains are also made during an epidemic, by mutation. Today, evolution enters the model.

transcript.title: The mutation matrix
transcript.text: Every transmission copies the pathogen, and copies can carry mistakes. Most changes do nothing. A few produce a new strain. In the model, a mutation matrix Q answers one question: when strain i transmits, what's the chance the new infection is strain j? Usually it's i again. With a small probability, mu, it's the next strain on a ladder. Mutation doesn't change how many new infections happen. It only changes which strain they are.

transcript.title: A ladder of strains
transcript.text: Our ladder: four strains, each escaping immunity to the ones before it, and each a bit more transmissible, with R₀ of two, 2.2, 2.4 and 2.6. Only strain one is there at the start. With no mutation: one wave, and it's over. Eighty percent infected. With one mutation in a million transmissions, each new strain takes off in turn: four waves, around days ninety one, one ninety, two sixty five and three twenty seven. With more mutation, the strains arrive sooner and the waves merge. At one in a thousand, all four strains together make one long wave. And each tenfold increase in mutation brings the next strain only about twenty four days sooner. In these equations, the wait depends on the logarithm of the mutation rate.

transcript.title: Chance decides emergence
transcript.text: But there's a catch. In the equations, a new strain exists from day one, as a tiny fraction of a person, and it grows smoothly. Real emergence is a matter of chance. A brand new mutant starts as a single case. And like any first case, it often fizzles. From Module three: it survives with a chance of about one minus one over its reproduction number. We checked this with four thousand simulated chains of cases. With a reproduction number of two, fifty one percent survived, against fifty percent in theory. With 1.2, seventeen percent.

transcript.title: Fewer infections, fewer variants
transcript.text: So successful new strains appear at a rate of: the mutation rate, times the number of transmissions, times the chance each mutant survives. Take a town of a million, and a variant that's made once in a million transmissions and would survive half the time. If the epidemic runs with R₀ of three, about nine hundred forty thousand people get infected, and there's a thirty eight percent chance a new variant takes hold. Hold R₀ to 1.3, and it's about four hundred twenty thousand infections and a nineteen percent chance. Fewer infections mean fewer chances to mutate. Controlling spread also slows evolution.

transcript.title: Measuring diversity
transcript.text: To follow diversity, count strains in a smarter way: take the Shannon diversity of the strain mix, and turn it into an effective number of strains. One strain dominating gives one. Two equally common strains give two. In our run with one mutation in a hundred thousand, the effective number rises to about two at each handover, and falls back as the new strain takes over.

transcript.title: Messier evolution
transcript.text: Real evolution is messier. Gains in transmission and immune escape come together, strains can recombine, and selection depends on the immunity left by earlier waves. Genomic surveillance, in Module nine, is how we watch it happen.

transcript.title: Module 5 recap
transcript.text: That's Module five: strains side by side, immune history and cross-immunity, and mutation that makes new strains, with chance deciding which ones survive. Next, Module six: agent-based models, where we simulate every person.

episodes.title: Why agents? Their power and their cost
episodes.hook: Why simulate every person? We build agents with states, rules and neighbours, check that 10,000 average agents give back the SIR equations, show how spreading out susceptibility shrinks the epidemic, meet Rule 110 and what agents can compute, and count the cost of checking contacts.
episodes.takeaway: Average agents give back SIR; spread-out agents do not. Agents can compute anything, and their contact loops cost time.

transcript.title: From boxes to agents
transcript.text: Welcome to Module six. Until now, our models moved people between boxes. Today, every person gets a little program of their own. Why would we do that, and what does it cost?

transcript.title: What an agent is
transcript.text: An agent is one simulated individual. It has a state, like susceptible or infected, plus anything else we care about: age, a household, a timer. It has rules for what it does each step. And it has neighbors: the agents it can meet. A scheduler decides when the agents act. Run the rules, and the epidemic curve comes out at the end. Nobody writes it down in advance.

transcript.title: Agents give back SIR
transcript.text: First check: can agents reproduce what we already know? Ten thousand agents. Each infectious agent meets ten random people a day and infects each susceptible one with a chance of two and a half percent. It recovers with a chance of ten percent a day. That's R₀ of 2.5. We ran it forty times, starting from ten cases. On average, eighty nine percent of the town got infected. The equations say the same: eighty nine percent. The peaks landed between day forty six and day sixty; the equations put it on day forty nine. So with everyone average and everyone mixing, agents just give back the SIR model, with some noise on top.

transcript.title: Nobody is average
transcript.text: The point of agents is that nobody has to be average. Keep the same average susceptibility, but spread it out: some people are hardly susceptible, some very much. Now only sixty percent get infected, not eighty nine. The least susceptible fifth: fourteen percent infected. The most susceptible fifth: ninety six percent. The susceptible get infected early, and the wave runs out of fuel sooner. An average hides who drives the epidemic. Agents keep that information.

transcript.title: Rule 110 and what agents can compute
transcript.text: How far can agents go? All the way. Here's a row of cells, each zero or one. At every step, each cell looks at itself and its two neighbors, and a fixed table gives its next value. This table is called Rule 110. Starting from a single live cell, it builds these patterns. And Matthew Cook proved that Rule 110 can carry out any computation at all. Treat each cell as an agent, and you have an agent model that can do anything a computer can. That's good news for flexibility, and bad news for prediction. No general method can tell you in advance whether an arbitrary agent model will even stop. So in practice we reason about the models we actually build.

transcript.title: The cost of contacts, and what to report
transcript.text: And those models cost time. The naive way checks every pair of agents every day. In our town that's fifty million pairs a day, and about 7.9 billion over one epidemic. Our agents only checked their ten contacts, so the work followed the infectious agents: about eight hundred ninety thousand checks per run. Nearly nine thousand times less. Grow the town tenfold, and the pairs grow a hundredfold, while the contact checks grow only tenfold. On a contact network, the work follows the edges of infectious agents instead. So when you report an agent model, report its size: how many agents, how many contacts or edges, how many steps, and which loop dominates the time and memory.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: agents are individuals with states, rules and neighbors. With everyone average they give back the equations. Their power is heterogeneity and explicit contacts, and in principle they can compute anything. Their price is design effort and computing time. Next time: building one. How to handle time, who moves first, and the shape of the world the agents live in.

episodes.title: Building an agent-based model
episodes.hook: Three choices that look like programming details: the time step, the update order and the neighbourhood.
episodes.takeaway: The time step, the update order and the neighbourhood are modeling choices that change the epidemic.

transcript.title: Three choices
transcript.text: Three choices in an agent model look like programming details: how time moves, who acts first, and what counts as a neighbor. Today we'll see that each one can change the epidemic.

transcript.title: Time: steps or events
transcript.text: Time first. The simplest choice is fixed steps: every step, every agent gets a chance to get infected and a chance to recover. Same rules, same town, only the step size changes. Steps of a tenth of a day give a peak of twenty four percent on day forty nine, just like the equations. Daily steps: twenty five percent, on day fifty one. Weekly steps: thirty five percent, on day sixty three. The step itself is a modeling choice. If a lot can happen within one step, a fixed step distorts the result. The alternative is to jump from event to event, as in the Gillespie algorithm from Module three. That's exact, but in a town of ten thousand you handle about eighteen thousand events one by one. Tau leaping sits in between: it lumps the events of a short leap together.

transcript.title: Who acts first
transcript.text: Second: who acts first. A line of two hundred cells, infection at the left end, and every infected cell infects its neighbors for sure. If all cells update at once, from the old state, the front moves one cell per step. That's synchronous updating. Now update one cell at a time, left to right, letting each cell see the new state. In a single step, the infection runs across all two hundred cells. Go right to left, and it moves one cell per step again. With a fresh random order each step, the front moves about 1.7 cells per step. The theory says e minus one, 1.72. The same happens in an SIR town. When everyone acts at once, the peak comes on day fifty six. When agents act one by one in a random order, a person infected in the morning can pass it on that afternoon, and the peak comes on day forty eight. Neither is wrong. But the update scheme is part of the model, so choose it on purpose, shuffle the order if you go one by one, and report it.

transcript.title: Geometry
transcript.text: Third: geometry. On a grid, who is your neighbor? Four cells, up, down, left and right? Or all eight around you? With certain infection, after sixteen steps, four neighbors give a diamond of five hundred forty five cells. Eight neighbors give a square of one thousand eighty nine. With a thirty percent chance per neighbor: one hundred eighteen against five hundred seven. Grids suit fields and buildings. For people, a contact network often matters more than distance, as we saw in Module four. And for crowds in a room, agents can move in continuous space.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: steps or events, all at once or one by one, and which neighbors. Each choice changes the timing and the size of the epidemic. Next time: randomness. How to make a random model reproducible, and how to compare two policies without drowning in noise.

episodes.title: Randomness and reproducibility
episodes.hook: Where an agent model's dice come from.
episodes.takeaway: Seeds make runs reproducible; common random numbers make policy comparisons sharp; every richer rule needs data.

transcript.title: Dice everywhere
transcript.text: Agent models roll dice all the time. Today: where the dice come from, how to get the same run twice, and how to compare two policies when every run is different.

transcript.title: Seeds and reproducibility
transcript.text: Computers don't really roll dice. They use pseudo-random number generators: formulas that produce numbers that look random, starting from a seed. Same seed, same numbers, same run. We ran our two thousand agent town twice with seed forty two, and got exactly the same epidemic, agent for agent. Seed forty three gives a different one. So save your seeds. They are part of the result. And on parallel machines, give each process its own stream, or the runs depend on which process happened to be faster.

transcript.title: How different runs are
transcript.text: How different are the runs? Two hundred runs of the same town, R₀ of 1.5, five first cases. Twenty nine fizzled out early. The rest ended between forty five and sixty five percent infected, fifty eight on average. The spread of single runs was about four percentage points. The uncertainty of the average shrinks with the square root of the number of runs: 1.3 points with ten runs, 0.4 with a hundred.

transcript.title: Common random numbers
transcript.text: Now compare two policies. A town of four thousand with R₀ of two, and a policy that removes three percent of contacts. On average it saves about two percent of the town. Run each policy with its own random numbers, two hundred times, and pair the runs up. In thirty seven pairs, the policy looks harmful. Pure noise. Now use common random numbers: give both policies the same random numbers, agent by agent and day by day. Then only six pairs out of two hundred look harmful. The spread of the difference dropped from 2.1 points to 0.9. To get the same precision with independent runs, you'd need more than five times as many.

transcript.title: Richer agents
transcript.text: Finally, richer agents. Our agents follow fixed rules. Agents can also have beliefs, desires and intentions, they can learn from what happens to them, and lately some models even use language models to decide what an agent does. A small taste: let agents who met an infectious person in the last week cut their chance of getting infected in half. Same town, same R₀. The epidemic grows slower and lasts longer, and it reaches forty nine percent of the town instead of eighty. Behavior can matter as much as biology. But every new rule is a new assumption, and it needs data behind it.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: seeds make runs reproducible, many runs measure the noise, common random numbers make comparisons sharp, and richer rules add realism at the price of more assumptions. Next time: two real case studies, influenza in a structured town, and COVID with behavior and testing.

episodes.title: Two case studies: flu-like illness and COVID-19
episodes.hook: Two case studies in a toy town of our own, after the ideas of FRED and Covasim: a flu-like illness with households, schools and workplaces, an eight-week school closure, a COVID-like illness with presymptomatic spread and isolation delays, and behaviour that feeds back.
episodes.takeaway: Structure shows who is infected and where; delays decide what isolation can do; behaviour feeds back.

transcript.title: FRED and Covasim
transcript.text: Two famous agent models shaped how we study epidemics: FRED for influenza and Covasim for COVID. Today we take the main idea of each, and build a toy version ourselves.

transcript.title: Our toy town
transcript.text: FRED builds synthetic copies of real cities: households, schools and workplaces, where the agents meet every day. Covasim adds detailed infection stages, testing and behavior. Our numbers come from our own small town, not from those tools. Our town: four thousand five hundred seventy eight people in nineteen hundred households, fifty three school classes, one hundred sixty eight workplaces, and random meetings around town. The values are made up to show mechanisms.

transcript.title: A flu-like illness
transcript.text: First, a flu-like illness: two days before becoming infectious, then four infectious days. Forty four percent of the town gets infected. Children: sixty eight percent. Adults: thirty nine. Seniors: thirteen. And we can ask where infection happens: forty four percent at home, nineteen percent at school, thirteen percent at work, and twenty four percent around town. A model with one infected box can't answer that question. A town of agents answers it directly.

transcript.title: Closing schools
transcript.text: Now close the schools for eight weeks, starting on the day two percent of the town has been infected. While they're shut, the epidemic stays low. When they reopen, it comes back, with a peak of 1.4% infectious on day one hundred twenty eight, against 3.8% on day fifty one without closure. In the end, thirty percent infected instead of forty four. The closure lowered the total, but it mostly moved the wave. When to reopen is as important as when to close.

transcript.title: A COVID-like illness and isolation
transcript.text: Second, a COVID-like illness in the same town: three days before becoming infectious, then two infectious days before symptoms, then five more. Thirty five percent never get symptoms, and they're half as infectious. Sixty six percent get infected, and twenty seven percent of infections come from people who don't have symptoms yet. Now let symptomatic people isolate, with eighty percent following the advice. Isolating on the first day of symptoms: thirty four percent infected. One day later: forty four. Two days: fifty one. Four days: sixty. Every day of delay costs. And the faster people isolate, the more of what remains comes from people without symptoms: thirty nine percent with same-day isolation. That's the part waiting for symptoms can never catch.

transcript.title: Behaviour feeds back
transcript.text: Finally, behavior. Let people cut their work and town contacts as reported cases rise, reported a week late. The peak drops from twelve percent infectious to 8.6%, and the total from sixty six percent to forty nine.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: structure tells you who gets infected and where. Stages and delays decide what testing and isolation can do. And behavior feeds back on the epidemic, as in Module two, now inside each agent. Next time: designing your own agent model, step by step.

episodes.title: Designing your own simulation
episodes.hook: Seven steps for designing an agent-based epidemic model: a question that names its output, the coarsest agents that work, contacts by setting, stage durations with the right shape, interventions as rule changes, a deliberate start, and enough runs.
episodes.takeaway: Seven steps: a question with an output, coarse agents, contacts by setting, stage shapes, rules, a deliberate start, enough runs.

transcript.title: Seven steps
transcript.text: Building an agent model is a chain of decisions. Today, seven steps that keep each decision tied to the question you're asking.

transcript.title: A question that names its output
transcript.text: Step one: a question that names its output. What quantity, in which population, over what time, compared with what? And what must the model reproduce before you trust it? How do schools affect transmission is too vague. How much does closing schools for eight weeks change infections among adults over two hundred days, is a question a model can answer. And ask whether you need agents at all. If everyone can be treated as average, a compartmental model is clearer and faster.

transcript.title: Agents and contacts
transcript.text: Step two: the agents. Choose the coarsest agent that still expresses the mechanism: people, households or places. Then their state: health state, time in that state, age, household. Step three: who meets whom. If your intervention acts on a setting, like closing schools, you need contacts organized by setting.

transcript.title: Stage durations
transcript.text: Step four: the illness itself, and how long each stage lasts. Same average durations, two days before becoming infectious and four infectious days, but three shapes. Memoryless, exponential durations: the peak comes on day seventy two, at 2.5% infectious. Four stages in a row: day fifty four, at 3.9%. Fixed durations: day forty eight, at 4.4%. Part of the reason: with exponential durations, many infections are very short and a few very long, and the long ones spend extra days on family members who are already infected. If timing matters to your question, the shape matters.

transcript.title: Interventions as rule changes
transcript.text: Step five: behavior and interventions, written as rule changes. Vaccination lowers susceptibility. Isolation removes contacts. Masks lower the chance per contact.

transcript.title: The starting point
transcript.text: Step six: the starting point. Who lives where, and who the first cases are. We started outbreaks with two cases, a hundred times each. Two children in one school class: sixty seven outbreaks took off, and they reached two percent of the town on day twenty nine on average. Two random adults: fifty seven took off, day thirty. Two seniors: twenty seven, day thirty three. Where the first cases are changes whether an outbreak starts, and how fast. Treat it as a modeling decision, not a detail.

transcript.title: Outputs and how many runs
transcript.text: Step seven: run and collect. Decide in advance what you log and how often. Logging everything slows the model and invites fishing for results. And decide how many runs you need. Single runs of our town spread by about two percentage points. To pin the average down to plus or minus one point, you need fourteen runs. For half a point, fifty three.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: a question with an output, the coarsest agents that work, contacts by setting, stage durations with the right shape, interventions as rule changes, a deliberate start, and an output plan with enough runs. Next time: how sensitive the answer is, and the ethics and risks of putting these models to use.

episodes.title: Sensitivity, ethics and policy risk
episodes.hook: How much to trust an agent model: we split uncertainty into inputs and chance, show why local sensitivity needs coupled runs, measure how easily people in a synthetic town can be singled out, look at who carries the burden, and discuss policy risk.
episodes.takeaway: Split uncertainty into inputs and chance, couple runs for sensitivity, protect privacy, report by group, and don't let detail pass for certainty.

transcript.title: How much to trust the number
transcript.text: An agent model has dozens of uncertain inputs, and it gives a different answer every run. How much should anyone trust its number? And what can go wrong when it's used?

transcript.title: Inputs or chance
transcript.text: The spread in the output has two sources. Inputs we don't know exactly, and chance: same inputs, different runs. The total variance splits into the variance of the average across inputs, plus the average of the run-to-run variance. We drew thirty settings for school and town transmission, each between seventy and one hundred thirty percent of our values, and ran each eight times. The inputs explain forty five percent of the variance; chance explains the rest. Ninety percent of runs ended between thirty four and fifty one percent infected. So report that range, not one run's number. And the split tells you where to spend effort: on better data for the inputs, or on more runs.

transcript.title: Local sensitivity
transcript.text: Local sensitivity asks a narrower question: nudge one input, and how much does the output move? We raised town transmission by five percent and measured the change in the share infected. With independent runs, eleven of thirty estimates came out negative, as if more transmission meant fewer infections. The lowest was minus 0.8 and the highest 0.9, plus one wild value from a run that fizzled. With common random numbers, all thirty landed between zero and about 0.6. The average was 0.26. Couple the runs, or the noise swamps the effect. Inputs that jump, like schools open or closed, are compared as scenarios. Global methods such as Morris and Sobol come in Module eleven.

transcript.title: Privacy
transcript.text: Now the ethics. Realistic agents are built from data about real people, and realism can expose them. Even in our made-up town, an exact age, a household size and a neighborhood single out one person for a quarter of the town. Group ages into ten year bands, and that falls to 0.4%. Coarsen, aggregate, and treat synthetic populations as sensitive data.

transcript.title: Who carries the burden
transcript.text: The burden isn't even, either. In our flu-like runs, nineteen percent of people living alone got infected, against eighty percent of people in six person households. And interventions land unevenly too: closing schools costs some families far more than others. So report results by group, not only the total.

transcript.title: Policy risk
transcript.text: Finally, policy risk. A detailed model looks precise, and its output can be given more authority than its data support. State the question it was built for, the range of outcomes, and what it cannot tell you.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: So: split the uncertainty into inputs and chance, couple runs when you measure sensitivity, protect the people behind the data, look at who carries the burden, and don't let detail pass for certainty. That closes Module six. Next, in Module seven, we turn from simulating epidemics to learning them from data.

episodes.title: Counts are not cases
episodes.hook: Cases are not infections.
episodes.takeaway: Cases are a filtered, delayed, noisy view of infections; counts scatter like a negative binomial, not a Poisson.

transcript.title: Counts are not cases
transcript.text: A dashboard says two thousand cases today. That's not the number of infections, and it isn't even an exact count of cases. Welcome to Module seven: models built from data, starting with the bridge between the epidemic and the numbers.

transcript.title: A simulated system with a known truth
transcript.text: To keep things honest, this module uses a simulated surveillance system, so we know the truth. A town of five million, two waves. One in four infections becomes a reported case, about six days after infection, once a test comes back. Over the year: about one and a half million infections, and three hundred sixty thousand cases. Cases are a filtered, delayed and noisy view of infections. The observation model describes that filter.

transcript.title: How noisy counts are
transcript.text: Start with the noise. Say we expect two thousand cases on a day. If counts were Poisson, almost every day would land between one thousand nine hundred twenty seven and two thousand seventy four. Real counts scatter far more: clusters, testing campaigns, batches of results. In our system the spread follows a negative binomial: the variance is the mean plus the mean squared over k, with k of thirty. Then the same day's ninety percent range is one thousand four hundred thirty five to two thousand six hundred forty one. Check it against the truth. Poisson ranges held the count on only forty one percent of days. Negative binomial ranges, on ninety one percent, as they should. So a jump of two hundred cases can be pure noise. Choose the observation model before you read meaning into the data.

transcript.title: Finding the dispersion
transcript.text: How do you find k? Plot the spread against the mean. Poisson is a straight line: variance equals mean. Our counts curve upward, and a fit gives k of about thirty five; the true value is thirty. Noise that grows with the mean is also why many models work on the log scale. There, a ten percent wobble looks the same at a hundred cases as at ten thousand.

transcript.title: Zeros
transcript.text: Zeros need care too. A zero can mean no cases, a closed lab, or a missing report. In our quiet weeks, with less than one expected case a day, half of the days had zero cases: just what both models predict. So before reaching for a special zero-inflated model, check whether small means already explain the zeros.

transcript.title: The layers of an observation model
transcript.text: The full observation model has more layers: what share of infections are found, how long they take to be reported, and how reporting depends on the calendar. Next: the calendar. Weekday patterns and holidays, and how to keep them from fooling you.

episodes.title: Seasonality and reporting artefacts
episodes.hook: Why dashboards jump on Mondays: weekday and holiday reporting patterns, measured from the counts and recovered by a regression, why day-to-day growth is noise, and two ways to keep the calendar out of the epidemic.
episodes.takeaway: Weekday and holiday patterns come from reporting offices: compare like with like, or model the calendar.

transcript.title: Mondays and Sundays
transcript.text: Every Monday our dashboard jumps, and every Sunday it dips. The virus doesn't keep a calendar. The reporting offices do.

transcript.title: The weekly reporting pattern
transcript.text: In our simulated system, the offices report only seventy five percent of what arrives on Saturdays and fifty five percent on Sundays. The rest waits until Monday. Divide each day by its centered seven day average. Mondays come out at 1.69 times the weekly level. Saturdays drop to 0.74, and Sundays to 0.55. Monday alone carries about a quarter of the week's reports. A regression with a smooth trend and a factor for each weekday finds the same numbers, from the counts alone. And here is the giveaway: count the same cases by test date instead of report date, and the weekly pattern almost vanishes. Every weekday lands within seven percent of the weekly level. The pattern is made by reporting, not by transmission.

transcript.title: Growth from day to day
transcript.text: Why it matters: growth measured from one day to the next swings wildly. On the log scale its noise is about 0.5, enough to make a slow decline look like a sixty percent jump. Compare the same weekday a week apart instead, and the error in the daily growth rate drops to about 0.03. The same trap waits for anything built on daily counts. A reproduction number estimated from raw reports rises every Monday and falls every weekend, unless the weekday effect is removed first. Compare like with like: the same weekday, or a seven day average.

transcript.title: Holidays
transcript.text: Holidays are the same problem, once in a while. On our holiday, day one hundred twenty two, reports fell from six hundred nine to one hundred eighty nine, and the next day jumped to one thousand eighty nine. A seven day average absorbs most of it: the dip and the catch-up cancel inside the window. But comparing the same weekday a week apart is fooled twice. The holiday looks like a seventy percent drop. And one week later, an ordinary day compared with the holiday looks like growth of more than double.

transcript.title: Decomposition and calendar terms
transcript.text: Two tools handle all this. The first: decompose the series into a trend, a weekly pattern and a remainder, for example with a smoother fitted in windows, and model the trend. On the log scale the weekly pattern becomes a set of additive weekday effects. The second: keep calendar terms, weekday and holiday indicators, inside the forecasting model itself, so it learns them together with the trend and carries them into its forecasts. Either way, model the reporting process, so you don't mistake it for the epidemic. Next: models that learn the dependence over time from the data. ARIMA, seasonal ARIMA, and state space models.

episodes.title: ARIMA, SARIMA and state-space models
episodes.hook: Forecasting case counts with ARIMA, seasonal ARIMA and state-space models: a rolling-origin backtest against simple baselines, honest prediction intervals, missing days, and the weak spot of every linear model, the turning point.
episodes.takeaway: Seasonal ARIMA beat simple baselines with honest intervals, but every linear model struggles at turning points.

transcript.title: Forecasting
transcript.text: So far we described the data. Now we forecast it. The classic tool learns how today's count depends on the last few days: ARIMA.

transcript.title: ARIMA and seasonal ARIMA
transcript.text: Three ingredients. Differencing: work with changes instead of levels, which removes a trend. Auto-regression: today's change depends on the last few changes. Moving average: today's surprise echoes for a few days. Seasonal ARIMA adds the same pieces at a lag of seven days, for the weekly pattern. We fit it to log counts, and pick the orders with an information criterion.

transcript.title: The rolling-origin backtest
transcript.text: Then the honest test, a rolling-origin backtest. Pretend it's day one hundred, fit only on the past, forecast two weeks, and compare with what happened. Move forward two weeks and repeat, seventeen times. Seasonal ARIMA missed by two hundred forty eight cases a day on average. Repeating the last value missed by three hundred thirty six. Repeating last week, by three hundred forty six. The weekly mean, by four hundred fifteen. Its eighty percent intervals caught the truth eighty five percent of the time. The wider intervals, meant to catch it ninety five percent of the time, did exactly that. The intervals also widen with the horizon. One day ahead the average miss was eighty five cases; two weeks ahead, four hundred forty eight. A forecast without honest intervals is half a forecast. And a model has to beat simple baselines before it earns any trust.

transcript.title: State space and missing days
transcript.text: State space models write the same idea as a hidden state, here the level and trend of log cases, plus noisy observations of it. The Kalman filter updates the state day by day. A bonus: missing days are no problem. We deleted fifteen random days and one whole week, and the model kept estimating through the gaps. On the missing days its error was about fifteen percent, no worse than on the days it saw.

transcript.title: Turning points
transcript.text: These linear models are strong baselines. Their weak spot is turning points: they extend the recent trend until the data prove them wrong. Forecasting from day two hundred fifty four, just after the second peak, the model expected about two thousand five hundred seventy cases two weeks later. The truth was one thousand one hundred eighty five: the wave had turned, and the past could not say so. Next: when late reports hide the present. Nowcasting under reporting delay.

episodes.title: Nowcasting under reporting delay
episodes.hook: Why the latest days always look low: reporting delay, the reporting triangle and right truncation, a simple nowcast that cuts the error from 37% to 12%, what happens when labs slow down, and Bayesian nowcasting.
episodes.takeaway: The latest days always look low because reports are late; a nowcast corrects them, if the delays stay the same.

transcript.title: The latest days always seem to fall
transcript.text: Look at the latest days on a dashboard, and cases often seem to be falling. Often they aren't. The reports just haven't arrived yet.

transcript.title: Delays and the reporting triangle
transcript.text: In our system, only eight percent of a day's cases are reported by the next morning, and fifty six percent within three days. Seeing them all takes two weeks. Write it as a reporting triangle: one row per test date, one column per delay. The most recent rows are still incomplete. Statisticians call it right truncation: the newest data are cut off before they are complete. On day one hundred fifty, the last test day showed twenty six cases. Two weeks later it had three hundred fifty two.

transcript.title: A simple nowcast
transcript.text: Counting only what has arrived, the last seven days look thirty seven percent lower than they finally turn out. On average, every time. Nowcasting fills in the triangle. Estimate the delay distribution from rows that are complete, then scale up each recent day by the share of its cases you expect to have seen so far. Our simple version cut the error for the last seven days from thirty seven percent to twelve. The nowcast is still a guess: the remaining cases arrive by chance, so the newest days carry the widest uncertainty. A good nowcast reports that uncertainty with the number.

transcript.title: When delays change
transcript.text: But it assumes the delays stay the same. Between days two hundred and two hundred forty, our labs slowed down: the average delay rose from 2.8 to 4.5 days. The nowcast, still using the old delays, fell short by thirty four percent. Better than the raw counts, at sixty one, but badly wrong just as the second wave was growing. And when the labs sped up again, the nowcast was still using the slow delays, and overshot by up to seventy percent. So watch the delays themselves, and estimate them from recent data.

transcript.title: Bayesian nowcasting
transcript.text: Bayesian nowcasting, such as the NobBS method, treats the whole triangle as data, lets the delays change over time, and gives an interval instead of one number. Either way, a nowcast is a layer before the forecast: correct the recent data first, then forecast from the corrected curve. Next: machine learning and deep learning forecasts, and when they help.

episodes.title: Machine learning and deep learning forecasts
episodes.hook: Machine learning against seasonal ARIMA on the same simulated data: turning a time series into a table, four learners in a rolling-origin backtest, errors by horizon and phase, and where deep learning fits.
episodes.takeaway: On one year of data the simplest learner did best; test every learner with rolling origins against simple baselines.

transcript.title: Learners against ARIMA
transcript.text: Machine learning wins competitions. Does it win at forecasting epidemics? Today four learners take on seasonal ARIMA, on the same simulated data.

transcript.title: From a series to a table
transcript.text: First, turn the time series into a table. Each row holds the last fourteen days of log cases, their weekly average, the weekday we're predicting, and how far ahead it is. The target is the count on that day. Then any learner can fit it: a ridge regression, a random forest, gradient boosted trees, and a small neural network. One model learns all horizons at once, because the horizon is one of the features. Another option is to forecast one day, feed it back in, and repeat; errors then pile up from day to day.

transcript.title: The backtest
transcript.text: Same honest test as before, with rolling origins: every week from day one hundred fifty to day three hundred twenty five. Twenty six forecasts, two weeks each. Average error, as a share of the cases: ridge regression twenty four percent, seasonal ARIMA twenty six, the neural network twenty seven, the random forest thirty, boosted trees thirty two. Repeating last week: thirty three. On one year of data, the simplest learner did best, and the fancier ones barely beat repeating last week. Machine learning needs data: longer histories, more places, more signals.

transcript.title: Horizon and phase
transcript.text: Errors grow with the horizon, and the ranking changes with it. One day ahead, seasonal ARIMA was best, missing by ten percent. Two weeks ahead it missed by forty seven, while the neural network missed by thirty three and ridge regression by thirty five. And they depend on the phase. When cases were falling toward small numbers, relative errors jumped: for seasonal ARIMA, from twenty three percent in growing weeks to thirty five in falling ones.

transcript.title: Deep learning
transcript.text: Deep learning goes further. Recurrent networks carry a hidden state through time, and gated versions like LSTMs choose what to remember. Temporal convolutions look back through fixed windows. Transformers use attention to weigh every past day. They shine when there are many series and many signals at once: regions, mobility, searches. On one short series they have little to learn from, and they overfit easily without careful regularization and early stopping. Whatever the learner, test it like a forecaster: only the past in training, rolling origins, and simple baselines to beat. Next: large language models, and how they can read the text around an epidemic.

episodes.title: Large language models in epidemiology
episodes.hook: How large language models can join an epidemic pipeline: as readers that fill a fixed form, with their weaknesses, a toy check showing how one plain rule catches most extraction slips, and the safeguards that keep people accountable.
episodes.takeaway: Use language models as readers with fixed forms, simple checks and a person for the hard cases.

transcript.title: Outbreaks as text
transcript.text: Much of what we learn about an outbreak first appears as text: bulletins, news, situation reports. Large language models read text. How should they join an epidemic pipeline?

transcript.title: A reader with a fixed form
transcript.text: A language model predicts the next word from the words before it. That lets it turn messy text into summaries, labels or structured records. The cautious way to use one: not as the forecaster, but as a reader. Give it a bulletin and a fixed form to fill in: disease, place, date, new cases, deaths, hospital pressure, source. Ask for nothing else.

transcript.title: Weaknesses
transcript.text: Its weaknesses are real. Answers change with the wording of the prompt, it can state facts that aren't in the text, and it drifts when reporting language changes. So never let its output flow straight into a model. Check it.

transcript.title: A toy check
transcript.text: A toy test, with our simulated counts as the bulletins. Suppose the reader slips on two percent of days: it drops a digit, adds a digit, or copies the cumulative total instead of the day's cases. Unchecked, the seven day average is off by more than twenty percent on about nine percent of days. Now add one plain rule: flag any value more than four times, or less than a quarter of, the median of the last two weeks, and send it to a person. The rule caught ninety two percent of the slips with no false alarms, and the average was badly off on fewer than one day in two hundred. Fixed forms, simple checks, trusted sources, and a person for the hard cases: that's how a language model earns its place.

transcript.title: Safeguards and other uses
transcript.text: Other safeguards work the same way. Answer only from trusted sources fed to the model, not from its memory. Process the output with fixed code, not more prompting. Log every input and output so a mistake can be traced. Language models can also summarize papers and help draft analysis code. They can sketch scenarios, too. And they can be asked for forecasts directly, but then they must pass the same rolling-origin test as any other model. The rule holds every time: they assist, and people stay accountable.

transcript.title: Module recap
transcript.text: That closes Module seven: observation models, calendars, linear models, nowcasting, machine learning, and language models. Next, in Module eight, we fit mechanistic models to data.

episodes.title: Fitting by least squares
episodes.hook: Fitting an epidemic model by least squares on a simulated outbreak with a known truth: the loss, weights and the log scale, and why fitting cumulative counts makes error bars far too small.
episodes.takeaway: Least squares recovers R0 2.5, but a fit on cumulative counts claimed ±0.004 when the real spread was ±0.15.

transcript.title: Model meets data
transcript.text: We have a model, and we have data. Which parameter values make the model match the data? Welcome to Module eight: parameter estimation and calibration.

transcript.title: One outbreak, known truth
transcript.text: All module long we use one simulated outbreak with a known truth. A town of one hundred thousand, R naught 2.5: a transmission rate beta of 0.25 per day, and ten infectious days on average. Forty percent of infections are reported, with extra noise. Over a hundred days, thirty four thousand eight hundred fifty one cases were reported. Now we pretend we don't know beta or gamma.

transcript.title: Least squares
transcript.text: Least squares: for any beta and gamma, run the model, subtract its curve from the data, square each difference, and add them up. The best parameters make that sum as small as possible. Squaring punishes big misses and keeps the sum smooth, so a solver can slide downhill. And when the noise is normal with a known size, least squares is exactly maximum likelihood. Our fit gives beta 0.249. Gamma comes out at 0.099, so R naught is 2.51, against a true 2.5. A least squares solver finds this in a fraction of a second.

transcript.title: Weights and the log scale
transcript.text: But counts are noisier when they are big. A day with a thousand cases wobbles far more than a day with ten, so plain least squares lets the peak dominate. Weights fix that: divide each difference by the size of noise you expect on that day. Or fit on the log scale, where a ten percent miss counts the same at any size.

transcript.title: The cumulative trap
transcript.text: Now a trap. Fitting the cumulative curve looks beautiful: smooth, with tiny residuals. But each day's total carries all the earlier days' errors, so the errors are not independent. We repeated the fit on two hundred new noisy datasets from the same truth. The cumulative fit claimed its R naught was good to plus or minus 0.005. The estimates actually spread by 0.15, and its ninety five percent intervals held the truth only five percent of the time. Fitting daily counts was more honest, but still too confident: its intervals held the truth seventy four percent of the time, because the noise model behind the error bars was too simple.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Least squares is the baseline: simple, fast, and often enough. Next: how to search when the landscape is rough. Grids, Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms and swarms.

episodes.title: Search strategies
episodes.hook: Searching for the best parameters: grid search and coarse-to-fine sweeps, the curse of dimensionality, Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms and particle swarms, raced on one outbreak.
episodes.takeaway: Global searches find the valley fast; none reliably polishes the last percent: hand over to a local method.

transcript.title: Searching a landscape
transcript.text: Least squares tells you what to minimize. It doesn't tell you how to search. When the landscape is rough, or each model run is expensive, the search strategy matters.

transcript.title: Grid search
transcript.text: The simplest search is a grid: try every combination. With forty one values for each parameter, that is one thousand six hundred eighty one model runs. The best grid point was still seven percent worse than the best fit, because the optimum fell between grid lines. Zooming in three times, coarse to fine, got within one percent with three hundred sixty three runs. A grid is also a map. It shows the valley, the flat directions and any second minimum at a glance. That makes it a great diagnostic, even when it isn't the final method.

transcript.title: The curse of dimensionality
transcript.text: But grids explode. One of our model runs takes 8.7 milliseconds. Ten values for each of two parameters is a hundred runs. With six parameters it's a million runs: two and a half hours. With eight, a hundred million runs: ten days.

transcript.title: Bayesian, genetic, swarm
transcript.text: Bayesian optimization spends runs carefully. It fits a statistical stand-in for the loss to the runs so far, with its uncertainty, and runs the model next where an improvement looks most likely. Genetic algorithms keep a population: the better candidates are selected, crossed and mutated. Particle swarms move a flock of candidates, each pulled toward its own best spot and toward the flock's best.

transcript.title: A race on one outbreak
transcript.text: We gave each method twenty independent tries on our outbreak. Getting within ten percent of the best fit took Bayesian optimization a median of forty seven runs, the genetic algorithm one hundred eighty two, and the swarm two hundred nine. Random guessing didn't get there in six hundred. Polishing the last percent was slow for all of them: only a third to a half of the tries got within one percent of the best fit inside their budgets. So global searches are best at finding the right valley. To reach the bottom, hand over to a local method.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: gradients and derivative-free refinement, the methods that finish the job.

episodes.title: Gradients and derivative-free refinement
episodes.hook: Local refinement: getting gradients, choosing a finite-difference step, why plain gradient descent crawls in a curved valley, Levenberg-Marquardt, BFGS and Nelder-Mead, and what noise does to a search.
episodes.takeaway: Curvature-aware methods reached the best fit in about 20 model runs; plain gradient descent was still 48% off after 1,500.

transcript.title: Into the valley
transcript.text: Global search finds the valley. Local refinement walks to the bottom of it. There are two families: methods that use gradients, and methods that don't.

transcript.title: Getting a gradient
transcript.text: A gradient says which way is downhill. You can get one by nudging each parameter and re-running the model, from sensitivity equations solved alongside the model, or by automatic differentiation. Nudging needs care. Too big a step, and you measure the slope of a whole stretch of curve: with a step of 0.01 in beta, the error was ten percent. Too small, and rounding takes over. Here the best step was about ten to the minus eight.

transcript.title: Descent and curvature
transcript.text: Plain gradient descent steps straight downhill. In a long, curved valley that's slow: it keeps crossing the valley instead of following it. From our starting point, after three hundred steps and one thousand five hundred model runs, it was still forty eight percent above the best fit. Methods that use curvature do far better. Gauss Newton, in its Levenberg Marquardt form, uses the structure of least squares, and reached the best fit in twenty one model runs. BFGS, which learns the curvature as it goes, got within one percent in twenty two.

transcript.title: Nelder–Mead
transcript.text: When gradients are unreliable, use a derivative-free method. Nelder Mead moves a triangle of three points: reflect the worst point through the others, expand if that helped, contract or shrink if it didn't. It got within one percent in fifty runs.

transcript.title: Noisy objectives
transcript.text: Stochastic models make every method's life harder. We ran the same parameters twenty times with new random numbers: the loss swung with a standard deviation of about four thousand eight hundred. Raising beta by five percent changed its average by only about three hundred. Along a slice of beta, the noisy loss had ten local minima. With the same random numbers at every run, it had two, and a local method could follow it. So average over repeated runs, reuse the same random numbers, or use a method built for noise.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: when there's no likelihood at all. Simulation-based inference, and state-space models that track hidden states.

episodes.title: Simulation-based and state-space inference
episodes.hook: Fitting models without a likelihood: approximate Bayesian computation on a stochastic town, tolerance and summaries, and a particle filter that tracks the reproduction number through a lockdown.
episodes.takeaway: ABC recovered R0 from simulations alone; a particle filter saw R fall below 1 six days after a lockdown.

transcript.title: No likelihood
transcript.text: Some models are easy to simulate, but impossible to write a likelihood for: agent-based towns, network epidemics, branching processes. You can still fit them.

transcript.title: Approximate Bayesian computation
transcript.text: Approximate Bayesian computation: draw parameters from a prior, simulate an outbreak, compare it with the real one, and keep the draws whose outbreaks look close enough. Our test: a random outbreak in a town of two thousand, with five first cases and R naught three. It produced one thousand eight hundred eighty six cases, with a peak of eighty three on day thirty.

transcript.title: What ABC learned
transcript.text: We drew fifty thousand random parameter pairs. Beta could be as low as 0.1, or as high as 0.6. Gamma could be as low as 0.05, or as high as 0.3. Seventeen percent of the simulated outbreaks fizzled out. We compared total cases, peak day and peak height, and kept the closest one percent: five hundred draws. Their R naught had a median of 2.7. Ninety percent of them sat between 2.2 and 3.9. The truth was three. Beta and gamma on their own stayed wide, and moved together, with a correlation of 0.93. The data pinned down their ratio, not each one.

transcript.title: Tolerance and summaries
transcript.text: The tolerance is a trade-off. Keep ten percent of the draws, and the interval is wide: it spans 1.7 up to 4. Keep only the closest fifty, and it shrinks to between 2.6 and 3.6. But then you need far more simulations to get enough draws. And the summaries decide what can be learned. A summary that ignores timing can't tell a fast epidemic from a slow one.

transcript.title: A particle filter
transcript.text: State-space models take another route. The epidemic is a hidden state that moves day by day, and the data are noisy readings of it. Unknown parameters can join the hidden state. A particle filter tracks it with thousands of guesses, called particles. Each day it moves every particle forward with the model, weights it by how well it explains today's count, and resamples. Our test: the reproduction number drops from 2.5 to 0.8 on day thirty five. With three thousand particles, the filter's ninety percent band fell entirely below one on day forty one, six days later. Its bands held the truth on eighty eight percent of days.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: calibration. Choosing targets, linking the model to the data, and designing the loss.

episodes.title: Targets, observations and loss design
episodes.hook: Calibration for a purpose: how the choice of target, the observation mapping and the loss change a model's answer about hospital beds, on a simulated outbreak.
episodes.takeaway: Same model, same data: four calibration targets gave 476 to 800 peak beds; the truth was 681.

transcript.title: Fit for a purpose
transcript.text: Estimation asks which parameters the data support. Calibration asks a more practical question: how do we tune this model so it's fit for a purpose?

transcript.title: A richer truth
transcript.text: This time the truth is richer than the model. The outbreak follows an SEIR model with four latent days and R naught 2.5. Testing ramps up from twenty to fifty percent of infections over forty days, and three percent of infections need a hospital bed for eight days. The analyst uses a simple SIR model and the first sixty days of data. The question: how many hospital beds will be needed at the peak?

transcript.title: Calibration targets
transcript.text: Choose the calibration target, and the answer moves. Fitting the whole case curve gave seven hundred twenty six beds. Only the first thirty days: eight hundred. Peak timing, peak height and the total: four hundred seventy six. Bed occupancy itself: five hundred eighty four. The truth was six hundred eighty one. Same model, same data, four answers. Choose targets that match the purpose, and check the result on the quantity that matters.

transcript.title: The observation mapping
transcript.text: The observation mapping links model states to what is measured. Here testing ramped up, so part of the early growth in cases was just more testing. Assuming a constant reporting share, the fitted growth rate was 0.149 per day. With the ramp in the mapping, 0.130. The truth was 0.126.

transcript.title: Loss design
transcript.text: The loss decides which errors you accept. With plain squared errors the peak dominates, and the early days were off by a hundred and seven percent on average. Weighting by the expected noise brought that to seventy five percent, and the log scale to fifty eight, at the cost of a worse peak. And because the model is wrong, each loss gave a different R naught. Plain squares said 2.35. The weighted loss said 3.5, and the log scale 7.4. None of them is the truth, which was 2.5. Constraints and penalties help: keep rates in plausible ranges, and treat a parameter that runs into its bound as a warning. Some of our fits pushed the infectious period to the fifty day limit we allowed.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: identifiability, misspecification, and the diagnostics that tell you whether to trust a calibration.

episodes.title: Identifiability and diagnostics
episodes.hook: Can you trust a fit? Identifiability valleys and profiles, outside information, parameters that never separate, misspecification, stress tests and multi-objective trade-offs.
episodes.takeaway: Early data measure growth, not R0; a good fit is not proof: check parameters, profiles and unseen data.

transcript.title: Fits that say nothing
transcript.text: A fit can look perfect and still say nothing about a parameter. That's identifiability, and checking it belongs in every calibration.

transcript.title: The valley and the profile
transcript.text: Fit our outbreak using only its first twenty five days. The loss map shows a long, flat valley: many pairs of beta and gamma fit almost equally well. A profile makes it precise: fix gamma, refit beta, and see how much worse the fit gets. With twenty five days, gamma could be anywhere from 0.04, the edge of what we tried, to 0.22, and R naught anywhere from 1.6 to 5.1. But the growth rate, beta minus gamma, was pinned between 0.136 and 0.163. Early data measure growth, not R naught. With all hundred days, R naught narrowed to 2.2 to 2.6.

transcript.title: Breaking ties
transcript.text: Outside information breaks the tie. A prior saying people stay infectious for about ten days, give or take two, gave R naught 2.3 from the same twenty five days. Some pairs never separate. Fit the reporting share and the population size together, and their estimates were correlated at almost exactly minus one (−0.997). Only their product, the number of cases that could ever be reported, is identified.

transcript.title: Misspecification
transcript.text: Misspecification is subtler. We fitted an SIR model to data from an SEIR outbreak. The fit looked fine, and its residuals showed no pattern. But it pushed the infectious period to the fifty day limit, and gave R naught 8.1. The truth was 2.5. The right model fitted only a little better. So a good fit is not proof: check whether the parameters make sense, and test on data the fit didn't see.

transcript.title: Stress tests and trade-offs
transcript.text: Stress tests help. We refitted on windows from thirty to seventy days: R naught moved between 1.8 and 2.6, and the forecast peak between nine hundred twenty one and one thousand one hundred ninety three cases a day. The truth was one thousand one hundred seventy four. And when targets conflict, show the trade-off. Fitting cases alone and fitting bed occupancy alone gave very different parameters. The weightings in between trace a curve of compromises, and picking a point on it is a decision, not a fit.

transcript.title: Module recap
transcript.text: That closes Module eight: least squares, search, refinement, simulation-based inference, calibration and its diagnostics. Next, in Module nine: the data streams themselves, from surveillance to genomes.

episodes.title: Surveillance as measurement, and mobility data
episodes.hook: Surveillance as a measurement process: reporting delays and a changing reporting share, why cases can fall while infections rise, correcting serosurveys for imperfect tests, and how phone-based mobility data can mislead.
episodes.takeaway: Cases are infections seen through delays and a changing reporting share; correct serosurveys for test errors; phone data count only the phones they see.

transcript.title: The end of a pipeline
transcript.text: A case count is not a thermometer reading of the epidemic. It's the end of a long pipeline. Welcome to Module nine: the data streams, and what each one really sees.

transcript.title: Infections and cases
transcript.text: Our simulated city has a million people, an epidemic, a lockdown on day sixty two and a relaxation on day one hundred ten. We know every infection: seventy one thousand in all. An infection becomes a case only if someone notices: symptoms after about five days, then a test and a report about four days later. Cases arrive eight days after infection on average, and only a share is ever found. That share changes. Here testing grew from fifteen to thirty five percent of infections, and then a policy change on day one hundred fifty cut it to twenty. Overall, only twenty two percent of infections became cases.

transcript.title: When testing changes
transcript.text: Watch what the policy change does. In the week after it, infections grew by more than two percent a day, while cases fell by about one percent a day. For eleven days, cases fell while infections rose. So model the measurement: write the infections, then the delays and the reporting share that turn them into data.

transcript.title: Serosurveys
transcript.text: Serosurveys measure past infection directly: test a random sample for antibodies. But tests make mistakes. With ninety percent sensitivity and ninety eight and a half percent specificity, false positives dominate when few people are truly positive. On day forty, when only 0.03 percent had been infected, a survey of two thousand people would find about one and a half percent positive: fifty times too many. The standard correction subtracts the false positive rate. Then it divides by the sum of sensitivity and specificity, minus one. On day one hundred ninety, corrected surveys ranged from 3.9 to 5.8 percent, around the truth of 4.8. Cases alone said 1.4.

transcript.title: Mobility data
transcript.text: Mobility data tell us how places connect: who travels where, and who mixes with whom. Phone data are the richest source, but they count only the phones they see. Our test: an outbreak starts in a small town whose residents make a thousand trips a day to the city. Only eight percent of the town's people use the phone company that shares data, against twenty eight percent nationally. Scaled up, the data show two hundred eighty trips. With the true flows, the city passes one infectious person per ten thousand on day twenty seven. With the phone flows, the model says day thirty two: five days of warning that don't exist. And a drop in visits is not the same as a drop in contacts: the link between them has to be estimated. Treat mobility as an input with its own uncertainty, and protect the privacy of the people behind it.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: genomes. How sequences reveal new variants, and how sampling shapes what they can tell us.

episodes.title: Genomics: from sequences to transmission
episodes.hook: Genomic surveillance as an observation model: lab capacity, how many genomes it takes to spot a new variant, estimating its growth advantage, and what biased sampling does and doesn't distort.
episodes.takeaway: Fifty genomes a week found a new variant around day 31, five hundred around day 10; a constant sampling bias distorts its share, not its growth.

transcript.title: What genomes add
transcript.text: Counts tell you how many. Genomes tell you how infections are related: new introductions, local spread, and new variants.
