transcript.title: Sequencing as an observation model
transcript.text: From a patient sample to a lineage takes a pipeline: sequencing reads, alignment to a reference, a consensus genome, and a place on the family tree. Each step can fail, or bias what survives. And which samples get sequenced is an observation model of its own. The number of genomes depends on infections, but also on lab capacity, and on who decides what to sequence. In our city, labs sequence ten percent of cases, at most eighty a week. For seven weeks around the peak the cap was binding: in the busiest week, only six percent of cases were sequenced.

transcript.title: Lineage frequencies
transcript.text: Lineage frequencies are the workhorse. Suppose a new variant grows seven percent a day faster than the rest, on the log odds of its share, starting from one infection in a thousand. After eight weeks it's still under five percent of infections. Sequence fifty random cases a week, and the first variant genome typically turns up around day thirty one. Sequence five hundred a week, and around day ten. Now estimate its advantage from eight weeks of data. With fifty genomes a week, the ninety percent range was huge: 0.01 at the bottom, 0.41 at the top. With five hundred genomes a week, it tightened to between 0.05 and 0.09, around the true value of 0.07.

transcript.title: Biased sampling
transcript.text: Next, bias the sampling. Suppose travelers' samples are sequenced first, so the variant is three times as likely to be sequenced. Its share looks like ten percent when it's really about four. Yet the estimated advantage stays at 0.07: a constant bias shifts the log odds, not their slope. If the targeting starts halfway through, though, the advantage comes out at 0.09, about a quarter too high. So know how the samples were chosen, and keep that choice constant, or model it.

transcript.title: Beyond frequencies
transcript.text: Genomes can do more: count separate introductions, tell local spread from new seeding, and date when lineages arose. Those methods build transmission trees, and they need the same care about sampling.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: signals from beyond the clinic. Wastewater, searches, and pharmacy sales.

episodes.title: Wastewater, syndromic and pharmacy signals
episodes.hook: Signals beyond the clinic: wastewater (shedding, dilution, normalization), syndromic and search data that drift, pharmacy sales that aren't specific, and combining streams around one hidden epidemic.
episodes.takeaway: Wastewater turned 6 to 9 days before reported cases and ignored a testing cut; combining streams beat any one alone.

transcript.title: Beyond the clinic
transcript.text: Not everyone who's infected sees a doctor. But almost everyone uses a toilet. Signals from beyond the clinic can see what testing misses.

transcript.title: Wastewater
transcript.text: Wastewater first. Infected people shed viral genetic material into sewage, starting soon after infection. What reaches the treatment plant is the shedding of all infections combined, diluted by the flow. In our city, shedding peaks around six days after infection, samples come in three times a week, measurements are noisy, and on twenty seven rainy days the extra water dilutes everything. Dividing by a fecal marker, which the rain dilutes in the same way, corrects for the flow. Here it trimmed the error of the wastewater growth rate by about seven percent, from 0.042 to 0.039 per

transcript.title: Earlier, and blind to testing
transcript.text: After the first peak, infections started falling on day seventy two. The wastewater showed the turn on day. day seventy four with the correction and day seventy seven without it. Reported cases showed it only on day eighty three, six to nine days after the wastewater. And wastewater doesn't care about testing policy. In the two weeks after testing was cut on day one hundred fifty, infections grew 2.4 percent a day. Cases showed only 0.5. Wastewater showed 1.7.

transcript.title: Syndromic and pharmacy signals
transcript.text: Syndromic signals react fast too: emergency visits for fever, searches for symptoms. But they drift. Our search index followed symptom onsets with a correlation above 0.96 all year, yet it said the second wave was 2.8 times the first peak. The truth was 2. Pharmacy sales and absenteeism are broad, but not specific. At the peak, only twenty eight percent of our cold medicine sales came from this epidemic. The rest came from other illnesses.

transcript.title: Combining streams
transcript.text: The best use of these streams is together: one hidden epidemic, and many observation equations, each stream with its own delay, scale and noise, weighted by how much it can be trusted. Even the simplest version helps. Weighting the growth rates from cases and wastewater by their reliability, about three quarters cases and one quarter wastewater, gave a smaller error than either stream alone. No stream is the epidemic. Each one is a view of it, and good models combine the views.

transcript.title: Module recap
transcript.text: That closes Module nine. Next, in Module ten: interventions, from lockdowns to vaccines, and how to put them into a model.

episodes.title: Putting interventions into the model
episodes.hook: How interventions enter an epidemic model: a dial on the transmission rate, why lockdown timing matters as much as strength, contact matrices by setting (school, work, shielding), vaccination as a flow, and testing and isolation.
episodes.takeaway: A 60-day lockdown started on day 65 nearly halved deaths; started on day 10, it changed almost nothing. Shielding seniors cut deaths by 31% while barely moving R0.

transcript.title: Decisions inside the equations
transcript.text: A model that only predicts can't help a mayor decide. To help, the decisions have to be inside the equations. Welcome to Module ten: intervention policies.

transcript.title: A dial on transmission
transcript.text: The simplest way in is a dial on transmission. Distancing or masks multiply the infection rate by one minus u, where u, between zero and one, is how hard we push. Our town has a million people, an R₀ of 2.5 and a thousand hospital beds. With no action, eighty nine percent are infected, the beds overflow for forty five days, and about nine thousand one hundred people die. Turn the dial to thirty percent and leave it there. The peak falls by more than half, but the wave lasts longer, and the beds still overflow, now for fifty six days.

transcript.title: Timing
transcript.text: Timing matters as much as strength. Take a sixty day lockdown that cuts transmission by sixty percent, enough to hold R at one, and slide its start date. Started on day ten, it changes almost nothing: the epidemic simply waits. Started on day one hundred, after the peak, it's too late. The best start here was day sixty five, which cut deaths from about nine thousand one hundred to about four thousand nine hundred.

transcript.title: Who meets whom
transcript.text: Many measures act on who meets whom. Split contacts by setting: home, school, work, and everything else. A policy then scales parts of the contact matrix. In an age-structured version of our town, closing schools lowers R₀ from 2.5 to 2.1, yet deaths barely move. Shielding seniors hardly changes R₀ at all, but cuts deaths by thirty one percent. Closing schools, and cutting contacts at work and everywhere else in half, brings R₀ down to 1.3, and the share infected from eighty five to thirty nine percent.

transcript.title: Vaccines and isolation
transcript.text: Vaccination is different: it moves people out of the susceptible box. In the equations, it's a flow from S straight to immune. If half a percent of susceptible people gain immunity each day from day zero, forty six percent are eventually infected instead of eighty nine. Start on day sixty, after the wave took off, and eighty two percent are. Testing and isolation split the infectious box: people who are found move to isolation, where they no longer infect. If sixty percent of infections are ever found, isolating them within a day cuts R in half. It falls to 1.25. Find ninety percent and isolate within two days, and R drops below one. Speed and coverage both matter: what is never found can't be isolated.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: how to choose the best policy over time, with optimal control.

episodes.title: Optimal control for epidemics
episodes.hook: Optimal control for epidemics: the objective, Pontryagin's maximum principle and adjoints as shadow prices, the optimal lockdown path in an SIR town, smooth versus bang-bang policies, and re-planning with model predictive control.
episodes.takeaway: The optimal policy builds to about a 50% cut and tapers, landing near herd immunity; a plan made with the wrong R0 does no better than nothing until it is re-planned.

transcript.title: Hard and short, or gentle and long?
transcript.text: Lock down hard and short, or gently and long? Optimal control turns that question into mathematics.

transcript.title: The objective and the maximum principle
transcript.text: First, write down what we want to make small: the cost of infections over time, plus the cost of the measures, plus the infections still to come once we stop. Here the measure is a cut u in transmission, up to seventy percent, and its cost grows with the square of u. Pontryagin's maximum principle gives the conditions an optimal policy must meet. It adds a second set of equations, the adjoints, which run backwards in time. Each adjoint is a shadow price: the future cost of one more person in that state. The rule for the best cut follows: push harder when there are many infections, and when an infection costs much more in the future than a susceptible person does.

transcript.title: The optimal policy
transcript.text: Our town is a simple SIR model with an R₀ of 2.5. With no measures, eighty nine percent are eventually infected. The best constant cut, kept all along, is just thirteen percent, and it barely helps. The optimal policy starts small, builds to a cut of about fifty percent near the peak, then tapers slowly. The peak falls by half, and in the end sixty three percent are infected: close to the sixty percent where herd immunity is reached, with little overshoot. The best single strict lockdown costs about eight and a half percent more than the optimum. And two very different solvers agree: the adjoint method and a direct search over weekly cuts land within 0.02 percent of each other.

transcript.title: Smooth or bang-bang
transcript.text: The shape depends on the costs. If the cost of measures grows in proportion to u, instead of its square, the optimum becomes bang-bang: one strict lockdown, here from about day sixty to day one hundred twenty, and nothing else. And if infections weigh five times less, the best policy is gentle: never more than a twenty percent cut, for about a hundred days. So the answer is never just lock down or don't. It depends on what you count, and how you weigh it.

transcript.title: Model predictive control
transcript.text: One catch: the optimum is only as good as the model. Suppose the planner believes R₀ is two, when it's really 2.5. Following that plan to the end does no better than doing nothing. Re-planning every two weeks from the latest data recovers most of the loss, even with the wrong R₀. Re-estimating R₀ each time as well brings the cost back to the optimum. That's model predictive control: plan, act for a while, look again, and plan again.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: the economy enters the objective, and we choose who gets vaccinated first.

episodes.title: Health and economy; vaccination strategy
episodes.hook: Health and economy in one model: voluntary caution, the Pareto front of lockdown policies, why the choice is a value judgement, and vaccine priority by age: infections versus deaths, vaccine type and timing.
episodes.takeaway: Only 24 of 468 lockdowns were on the Pareto front; children first cut infections most, seniors first cut deaths most, and a later start doubled deaths.

transcript.title: Two bills
transcript.text: Every lockdown sends two bills: one paid in health, one in livelihoods. And every vaccine dose is a choice about who goes first.

transcript.title: An economy in the model
transcript.text: Our town again, now with an economy. A lockdown that cuts transmission by sixty percent costs thirty percent of that day's output. And people don't wait for orders: as hospital beds fill, they cut their contacts on their own. So doing nothing isn't free. With no lockdown, caution alone cut the share infected from eighty nine to seventy two percent, and cost about 2.4 percent of a year's output.

transcript.title: The Pareto front
transcript.text: Now try four hundred sixty eight lockdowns, with different strengths, start dates and lengths. Each one is a point: economic loss across, deaths up. Most are wasteful: another policy has both fewer deaths and a smaller loss. Only twenty four points are left. They form the Pareto front, the set of honest compromises. Which point to pick depends on how a death is weighed against output. That's a value judgement, not a calculation. Count a death as twenty years of one person's output, and a short, moderate lockdown wins. Count it as a hundred years, and a longer one does. And if a vaccine arrives on day two hundred, the picture changes. At the higher weight, the best choice is to suppress hard from day ten until the vaccine: deaths almost vanish, at a cost of seventeen percent of a year's output.

transcript.title: Who gets vaccinated first
transcript.text: Now, vaccines. In a well-mixed town, an R₀ of 2.5 means sixty percent must be immune for herd immunity. With a vaccine that's ninety percent effective, that's sixty seven percent coverage. But people differ. In our age-structured town, five thousand doses a day arrive from day thirty, four hundred thousand in all. Who should go first? To cut infections, vaccinate those with the most contacts: children first gave the fewest infections. To cut deaths, protect those most at risk: seniors first gave about thirteen hundred deaths, against about thirty two hundred for children first. If the vaccine mainly prevents severe disease rather than infection, the indirect protection fades: every order gave about the same number of infections, and seniors first was still best for deaths. And speed counts. Starting the same campaign on day sixty, instead of day thirty, doubled the deaths.

transcript.title: No universal ranking
transcript.text: The best order isn't a universal ranking. It depends on the vaccine, the contacts, the timing, and what you choose to minimize.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: interventions in space and on networks, policies that react to data, pathogens that evolve, and what real epidemics taught us.

episodes.title: Space, networks, strains and real use cases
episodes.hook: Interventions in space and time: how much time travel cuts buy, trigger policies and the cost of data lags, drug resistance under treatment pressure, and lessons from 1918, SARS, Ebola and COVID-19.
episodes.takeaway: A 99% travel cut bought four weeks; a 12-day data lag raised peak beds from 213 to over capacity; heavy treatment handed 95% of infections to a resistant strain.

transcript.title: Where you act
transcript.text: Where you act matters as much as how hard. And the pathogen can answer back.

transcript.title: Travel cuts
transcript.text: Six cities: a hub of two million, and five towns on a ring, linked by daily travel. An outbreak starts in one town. With no restrictions, the hub passes one infectious person in ten thousand on day thirty eight. Cutting all travel by ninety percent delays that to day fifty one. Even a ninety nine percent cut only reaches day sixty six, and in the end the same eighty nine percent are infected. Cut only the hub's links, and the hub is delayed just as much, but the neighbouring towns still catch it on day thirty eight, along the ring. Infection follows every path that's left open. Travel restrictions buy time, here about two weeks per tenfold cut. Time is worth a lot, if you use it to prepare.

transcript.title: Policies that react to data
transcript.text: Real policies react to data: measures go on when a signal passes a threshold, and off when it falls. Here, a seventy percent cut goes on above fifteen hundred new infections a day, and off below five hundred. If we could see infections the day after they happen, hospital beds would peak at two hundred thirteen, a fifth of capacity. With the four day lag of wastewater, three hundred fifty two. With the eight day lag of reported cases, six hundred eleven. With the twelve day lag of hospital admissions, the beds overflow. The lag also makes the response cruder: fewer, longer lockdowns, and almost twice the deaths in the first year.

transcript.title: Pathogens answer back
transcript.text: Pathogens evolve, and our measures shape the selection. Suppose an antiviral cuts the infectious period of treated people in half. A resistant strain shrugs it off. It spreads ten percent less well, but the drug can't touch it. Treating sixty percent of infections cut total infections by almost a fifth, but a third of them were resistant. Treating ninety percent made the resistant strain dominant by day ninety: ninety five percent of infections, and nearly as many in total as with no treatment. Vaccines that stop disease but not infection raise similar questions: in poultry, such vaccines have let more virulent strains of Marek's disease keep spreading. Evolution-aware policy counts tomorrow's strains, not just today's cases.

transcript.title: What real epidemics taught
transcript.text: Real epidemics teach the same lessons. In 1918, American cities that acted early and kept their measures in place generally saw lower peaks of death. With SARS in 2003, faster isolation after symptoms helped bring transmission down. In West Africa in 2014, Ebola showed that isolation beds and safe burials must scale up fast enough to keep pace. And COVID-19 turned every idea in this module into a daily decision: timing, triggers, vaccine priorities and new variants.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: That closes Module ten. Next, in Module eleven: uncertainty, sensitivity, and how to compare models.

episodes.title: Where uncertainty comes from
episodes.hook: Where uncertainty comes from: chance, parameters, measurement, model structure, scenarios and computation, added one layer at a time to the same simulated epidemic, and how much each one widens the forecast.
episodes.takeaway: Chance alone moved the peak by 17 days; unknown parameters stretched that to 43; adding measurement, structure and scenarios widened it further.

transcript.title: A guess dressed up as a fact
transcript.text: A forecast without uncertainty is a guess dressed up as a fact. Welcome to Module eleven: where uncertainty comes from, and how to measure it.

transcript.title: Chance
transcript.text: Start with chance itself. Run the same epidemic, with the same parameters, two thousand times in a town of twenty thousand. The final size barely moves: about ninety one percent every time. But the peak day ranges from day forty seven to day sixty four, depending on how the first chains of infection happen to go. That's process uncertainty: the randomness of who meets whom. It's aleatory, so better data won't remove it.

transcript.title: Parameters
transcript.text: Now admit we don't know the parameters exactly. Let R₀ be anywhere from two to three. Let the infectious period last eight days, twelve days, or anything between. The earliest peak now comes on day thirty eight. The latest comes on day eighty one. And the peak height more than doubles across the range. Splitting the variance of the peak day, about four fifths came from not knowing the parameters, and one fifth from chance. Parameter uncertainty is epistemic: better data can shrink it.

transcript.title: Measurement, structure, scenarios
transcript.text: Then the measurement. We see only twenty to forty percent of infections, about six days later, with noise on top. The reported peak arrives about five days after the real one. Its height can be as low as about one hundred thirty cases a day, or as high as three hundred eighty. Next, the model itself. If half of our analysts add a latent period, with the same R₀, the range of peak days stretches out to day one hundred fourteen. Structural uncertainty never shows up inside any single model's intervals. And the future. If there's an even chance that people cut their contacts by thirty percent from day forty, the final size could be as low as fifty six percent, or as high as ninety four. That's scenario uncertainty: not a property of the virus, but of choices still to be made.

transcript.title: Computation, and the full stack
transcript.text: A sixth source completes the list: computation. Samplers, filters and approximations add their own error, and they can fail quietly. Each layer added uncertainty. Leave one out, and your intervals are too narrow, and your confidence is borrowed.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: when the data can't tell parameters apart. Identifiability and confounding.

episodes.title: Identifiability and confounding
episodes.hook: Identifiability and confounding: why three towns with the same first month of cases can have very different futures, how the generation interval changes R, sloppy parameters, and how a serosurvey breaks the tie.
episodes.takeaway: Three towns with the same first month of cases ended with 9,000 to 85,000 cases; one serosurvey pinned the reporting share to 29–32%.

transcript.title: A perfect fit, unknown parameters
transcript.text: A model can fit the data perfectly and still not know its own parameters. That's not a bug in the fitting. It's a limit of the data.

transcript.title: Reporting or infections?
transcript.text: There are two kinds of identifiability. Structural: with perfect, noise free data, could the parameters be pinned down at all? Practical: with the noisy, finite data we actually have, can they? Here's a classic tie. Picture three towns. The first reports ten percent of its infections. The second reports thirty percent, and the third reports ninety. Each starts with a different number of infections, chosen so that all three show the same reported cases for thirty days, within ten percent, which is less than the daily noise. Their futures differ enormously. The reported peaks fall twelve days apart, from day thirty eight to day fifty, and the totals run from about nine thousand up to eighty five thousand. The early curve fixes the product of reporting and infections, not either one.

transcript.title: The generation interval
transcript.text: Assumptions can confound too. To turn a growth rate into a reproduction number, you need the generation interval. The same epidemic, doubling every seven days, gives R of about one and a half if the interval is four days. Stretch the interval to ten days, and R becomes about two and a half.

transcript.title: Sloppiness
transcript.text: Even when every parameter is identifiable in principle, most combinations are barely constrained. Fit a five parameter SEIR model to sixty days of cases, and the loosest combination of parameters is about three and a half thousand times more uncertain than the stiffest. That's sloppiness. The stiff direction here is essentially the growth rate. Along the sloppy directions, parameters can move a lot while the fit barely changes.

transcript.title: Breaking the tie
transcript.text: How do you break a tie? Bring in data that sees what cases can't. From forty days of noisy cases, the reporting share could be anywhere from sixteen to thirty five percent. Add one serosurvey of two thousand people on day forty, and the range shrinks to between twenty nine and thirty two percent. The truth was thirty. Before you trust a parameter, ask: could different values tell the same story? If so, find data that tells them apart, or report the whole range.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: which inputs drive a model's output? The sensitivity toolbox.

episodes.title: The sensitivity toolbox: Morris and Sobol
episodes.hook: The sensitivity toolbox: local derivatives and why they depend on where you stand, Morris screening, and Sobol indices that split an output's variance among seven inputs, with what each costs.
episodes.takeaway: R0 alone explained 78% of the variance in the final size; the cut's start day mattered only through interactions; reporting mattered only for reported peaks.

transcript.title: Which inputs matter?
transcript.text: Seven uncertain inputs, three outputs we care about. Which inputs actually matter? Sensitivity analysis answers that, if you ask it the right way.

transcript.title: Local sensitivity
transcript.text: Our town is an SEIR model with a sixty day cut in contacts. The inputs: R₀, the latent and infectious periods, the reporting share, the first infections, how strong the cut is, and when it starts. The outputs: the share ever infected, the peak of reported cases, and the day of that peak. The quickest check is local: nudge one input by one percent and watch the outputs. At our baseline, a one percent rise in R₀ raises the final size by about 0.9 percent, and the peak of reported cases by almost seven percent. But local answers hold only near the point where you stand. Here the cut starts on day fifty, right at the peak, so the start day looks hugely important: one percent later raises the peak by four percent.

transcript.title: Morris screening
transcript.text: Global methods move all inputs across their whole ranges. Morris screening is cheap: it walks random paths through the input space, changing one input at a time, and records each effect. One hundred paths cost eight hundred runs. The mean size of those effects ranks the inputs; their spread flags curves and interactions. For the final size, R₀ ranks first by far. For the peak of reported cases, the reporting share comes a close second.

transcript.title: Sobol indices
transcript.text: Sobol indices go further: they split the output's variance among the inputs. The first order index is the share due to an input alone; the total index adds every interaction it takes part in. With about one hundred forty seven thousand runs, R₀ alone explains seventy eight percent of the variance in the final size. The start day of the cut explains almost nothing alone, yet its total index is fifteen percent: it matters only together with other inputs. And the reporting share has a total index of zero for the final size and the peak day, but thirty seven percent for the peak of reported cases. Sensitivity always depends on the question.

transcript.title: The toolbox
transcript.text: The toolbox, in order of cost. Local derivatives give a first look in about fifteen runs. Morris screens many inputs with hundreds of runs. Sobol apportions the variance, but needs tens of thousands of runs or more, or a fast emulator trained to stand in for the model. Sensitivity tells you where to spend effort: which input to measure better, and which to stop arguing about.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: comparing models, with scores, coverage, and fitness for purpose.

episodes.title: Comparing models: scores and coverage
episodes.hook: Comparing models for a purpose: why better in-sample fit can mean worse forecasts, AIC, rolling-origin backtests, proper scores like the weighted interval score, interval coverage, and simple ensembles.
episodes.takeaway: An overconfident forecaster had the same error as an honest one but covered the truth only 23% of the time; a simple blend scored best.

transcript.title: Best for what?
transcript.text: Which model is best? Wrong question. Best for what? Nowcasting, forecasting and explaining reward different things.

transcript.title: Fit is not foresight
transcript.text: First trap: in-sample fit. We fitted polynomials to twenty eight days of log cases. Each extra degree fitted the past better, but forecasts seven days ahead got worse. By degree five, they were typically off by a factor of about fourteen. Penalized criteria like AIC push back on complexity: here, AIC preferred the straight line. Better still, test a model the way you'll use it: forecast from many past dates, using only the data available on each date.

transcript.title: Proper scores
transcript.text: Then score the whole forecast, not just its middle. We backtested four forecasters on a simulated town with two waves, from twenty six dates, seven days ahead. A trend forecaster and an overconfident copy of it have the same median, and so the same average error. But the copy's ninety percent intervals caught the truth only twenty three percent of the time. The honest version: ninety six percent. A proper score, like the weighted interval score, rewards being both sharp and right. It ranked the overconfident copy behind the honest one: 9.5 against 7.9, lower is better. A very wide forecaster caught everything, and still scored worse: 9.9.

transcript.title: Calibration and ensembles
transcript.text: Calibration asks whether intervals mean what they say: ninety percent intervals should contain the truth about ninety percent of the time. Check it with coverage, and with histograms of where each observation falls within its forecast. Combining forecasters often helps. An equal blend of last week's level and the trend scored 6.5, better than either alone, with ninety six percent coverage.

transcript.title: Fitness for purpose
transcript.text: Finally, match the criteria to the decision. When running out of beds costs far more than having beds to spare, a model that captures the tail may beat one with a smaller average error. Uncertainty quantified, sensitivity explained, models compared for their purpose: that's what makes a model trustworthy.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: That closes Module eleven. Next, in Module twelve: the computer side of epidemic modeling.

episodes.title: Languages, libraries and architecture
episodes.hook: The computer side of epidemic modeling: one agent-based model written in plain Python, NumPy, JavaScript and C and timed, why tested libraries matter, how to keep a model's parts apart, and a planted bug that only a conservation check catches.
episodes.takeaway: The same model ran about 40 times faster in C than in plain Python loops, with the same answer; a planted bug left the infection curve perfect and was caught by a one-line conservation check.

transcript.title: Same math, different code
transcript.text: The same epidemic model can take a tenth of a second to run, or a few thousandths. Same math, different code. Welcome to Module twelve: the computer side of epidemic modeling.

transcript.title: One model, four languages
transcript.text: Choosing a language is a trade between how fast the code runs and how fast you can write it. We wrote one agent based model, ten thousand people for two hundred days, four times: in plain Python, in Python with NumPy, in JavaScript, and in C. C ran a whole epidemic in under four thousandths of a second. Plain Python loops took almost forty times longer. NumPy, which hands the loops to compiled code, came within a factor of two of C. JavaScript, which runs the labs on our website, was not far behind. And all four agreed: about ninety two percent of the town infected. That's the first rule: a faster version is only worth having if it gives the same answer.

transcript.title: Libraries
transcript.text: Libraries matter as much as languages. Well used solvers, random number generators and statistics packages have been tested by thousands of people. Writing your own is a great way to learn, and a risky way to publish.

transcript.title: Architecture
transcript.text: Then architecture. Keep the parts of a model apart: the transmission mechanism, the parameters, the observation model that turns infections into reported cases, the inference code, and the outputs. Each part can then be tested, swapped and reused. Settings live in files, not inside the code, so every run records exactly what it used: the parameters, the data version, and the random seed.

transcript.title: Test the model
transcript.text: And test the model, not just the code. Here's a bug we planted on purpose: one term in an SEIR model takes recoveries from the exposed group, instead of the infectious group. The infection curve looks perfect: same peak, same day. But people are quietly disappearing. By the end, the town has lost more than a third of its population. A one line check, does everyone still add up to the whole town, flags it at the very first step. Another check compares the final size with the formula from Module three; a correct model agrees to within a millionth. Checks like these, run automatically after every change, catch exactly the errors that look plausible.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: numerical stability, and how a bigger time step can make your epidemic go negative.

episodes.title: Numerical stability
episodes.hook: Numerical stability: Euler against Runge-Kutta on the SIR model, step sizes that push compartments below zero, stiff models and the solvers built for them, why a daily-step model is a different model, and exact Gillespie simulation against tau-leaping.
episodes.takeaway: Euler with 7-day steps overshot the peak by 60% and went below zero; Runge–Kutta with 4-day steps stayed within 0.1%. A stiff solver needed about 30 times fewer evaluations.

transcript.title: Right model, wrong solver
transcript.text: Your model can be right, and your solver wrong. The same equations, solved with a careless step size, can give the wrong peak, or even a negative number of people.

transcript.title: Euler and Runge–Kutta
transcript.text: Take our SIR town. R₀ is 2.5, and people stay infectious for five days. Solved with tiny steps, the epidemic peaks with twenty three percent of the town infectious, on day thirty two. Euler's method, the simplest solver, follows the slope for one whole step. With one day steps it overshoots the peak by six and a half percent. With seven day steps, by sixty percent, and the number infectious drops below zero. Runge Kutta of order four averages four slopes per step. With two day steps it lands within a hundredth of a percent of the peak; even with four day steps, within a tenth.

transcript.title: Stiff models
transcript.text: Some models are stiff: they mix very fast and very slow processes. Add a one hour triage step before hospital to our town. Euler now needs steps under two hours just to stay stable. With steps of a tenth of a day, the numbers swing and blow up. An adaptive solver built for smooth problems survives, but needs about eighteen and a half thousand evaluations for one year. Solvers built for stiff problems need about six hundred and forty, for the same answer: almost thirty times less work.

transcript.title: Daily steps
transcript.text: Discrete time models hide a quieter trap. A model that steps one day at a time is a different model, not an approximation. Turning the daily rates into daily probabilities stretched the average infectious time by half a day, to five and a half days. That quietly raised R₀ to 2.76. The continuous model had 2.5. The peak climbed too. It reached twenty seven percent instead of twenty three. Nothing crashed. The numbers were just different.

transcript.title: Exact and approximate randomness
transcript.text: Stochastic models have their own trade off. Gillespie's algorithm is exact: it simulates every single event. For a town of ten thousand, that's almost eighteen thousand events per epidemic. Tau leaping jumps ahead in fixed steps and draws many events at once. With steps of a tenth of a day, it matched the exact method closely. With four day steps, the final size rose to ninety six percent, where the exact answer is eighty nine. And most runs tried to remove more people than there were. So build in guards: no compartment below zero, everyone accounted for, and a check that a step half as long barely changes the answer.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: making it fast. Where the time goes, and how to win it back.

episodes.title: Making it fast
episodes.hook: Making epidemic code fast: profile first, replace an all-pairs contact search with a grid of cells, batch a thousand parameter sets into arrays, preallocate, store contact networks sparsely, exploit structure in the mixing matrix, and Amdahl's law for parallel computing.
episodes.takeaway: A grid of cells gave the same epidemic as checking every pair, 8.6 times faster for 2,000 people; batching was 85 times faster, and a sparse network needed 12 MB instead of 80 GB.

transcript.title: Measure first
transcript.text: Before you make code faster, find out where the time goes. The answer is rarely where you'd guess.

transcript.title: The obvious version
transcript.text: Our town of agents lives on a map: people infect neighbors within a short distance. The first version is the obvious one. Every day, every infectious person checks every person in town. A profiler measures where the time goes. For a town of two thousand, it pointed at one place: the pair check, called more than nine million times in a single epidemic, inside a loop over every pair.

transcript.title: A better algorithm
transcript.text: So change the algorithm. Divide the map into cells as wide as the contact distance; then each person checks only the nine cells around them. We fixed every random draw in advance, so both versions must give the same epidemic, to the last person. They did. For two thousand people, the grid ran about eight and a half times faster. And the gap keeps growing: the obvious version's work grows with the square of the town, the grid's only in proportion to it.

transcript.title: Work in bulk
transcript.text: Next, let the computer work in bulk. Running a thousand parameter sets one at a time took two and a half seconds. The same thousand as one batch of arrays took three hundredths of a second: eighty five times faster, with identical numbers. Small habits matter too. Growing an array one value at a time copies it again and again: about seventy times slower than filling an array made in advance.

transcript.title: Structure, sparsity, parallel
transcript.text: And use the structure of the problem. A contact network of a hundred thousand people, with about ten contacts each, stored as a full table, needs eighty gigabytes. Stored as a list of who knows whom: twelve megabytes. One step of the epidemic then takes about a millisecond. When people mix in proportion to their activity, the mixing matrix collapses into two vectors. For three thousand groups, the force of infection came out more than a thousand times faster, with the same result. Parallel computers help with the rest, but only with the part that can run in parallel. If a twentieth of the work is serial, sixty four cores give you about fifteen times, and no number of cores gives more than twenty. Measure first, fix the algorithm, then the habits, and check the answer after every step.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: Next: calibration at scale, when every run of the model costs real time.

episodes.title: Calibration at scale
episodes.hook: Calibration at scale: what a run costs and what that makes affordable, gradients from sensitivity equations against finite differences and Nelder-Mead on a 26-parameter fit, and Gaussian-process emulators with history matching for an expensive agent-based model.
episodes.takeaway: With exact gradients a 26-parameter fit took 75 runs instead of about 2,000; an emulator trained on 50 runs ruled out half of the settings in under a hundredth of a second.

transcript.title: Can you afford it?
transcript.text: Fitting a model means running it again and again. When one run takes seconds, the question is no longer how to fit it, but whether you can afford to.

transcript.title: The arithmetic of runs
transcript.text: Here's the arithmetic. Our SIR equations take about a hundredth of a second per run. Our agent town of sixteen thousand people, about two seconds. Twenty thousand steps of a Bayesian sampler: about three minutes for the equations, about eleven hours for the agents. A million runs for approximate Bayesian computation: a couple of hours, or about three weeks.

transcript.title: Gradients
transcript.text: So make every run count. Gradients help most: they tell the optimizer which way is downhill in every direction at once. We fitted a separate transmission rate for each of twenty six weeks to half a year of noisy cases. Without gradients, Nelder Mead used twenty thousand runs and still hadn't finished. With gradients from finite differences, a quasi Newton method finished in about two thousand. With exact gradients, from sensitivity equations solved alongside the model, it took seventy five. Automatic differentiation tools can build those derivatives straight from a model's code. We checked ours against finite differences: they agreed to about one part in a billion, at the right step size.

transcript.title: Emulators and history matching
transcript.text: When even that is too slow, train an emulator: a fast statistical stand in for the simulator. We ran the agent town fifty times, at well spread settings, and fitted a Gaussian process to the results. On sixty new runs, it predicted the share infected to within about seven points on average, and its ninety percent intervals caught eighty eight percent of the truths. Then history matching: rule out every setting the emulator says cannot reproduce the observed epidemic. Half of the ten thousand settings were ruled out in under a hundredth of a second; simulating them all would take about three hours. We checked twenty of the settings it kept, and four reproduced the epidemic. Not one of twenty ruled-out settings did. History matching doesn't finish the job. It shrinks the search, safely, so the expensive runs go where they can matter.

transcript.title: In this order
transcript.text: Correct first, then stable, then fast, and only then at scale. A speed up is worth nothing if the answer changes.

transcript.title: Next
transcript.text: That closes Module twelve. Next, the final episode: where epidemic modeling goes from here.

episodes.title: What comes next
episodes.hook: The closing episode: what each family of models taught us, the problems that come back whatever the model, and where epidemic modeling is heading: adaptive forecasts, many data streams together, checked language models, AI that helps, shared benchmarks and decision-focused models.
episodes.takeaway: No single model wins: mechanistic, statistical, machine-learning and simulation models answer different questions, and the future lies in combining them around real decisions.

transcript.title: The question
transcript.text: This course began with a plague in Athens. It ends with one question: where does epidemic modeling go from here?

transcript.title: What we built
transcript.text: First, look back at what we built. Compartmental models taught us to think in flows between states. Space, networks and strains showed that epidemics move, branch and evolve. Agents showed how a town's outcome grows out of many small choices. Data driven models showed that prediction can come from patterns, not only from mechanisms. Then fitting, surveillance, policy, uncertainty and computation turned all of these into tools you can trust, and taught you when not to. No single model wins. Mechanistic models explain. Statistical models keep us honest about the data. Machine learning finds patterns. Simulations show what can emerge. The skill is knowing which question each one answers, and letting them check each other.

transcript.title: Problems that come back
transcript.text: Some problems come back whatever the model. Epidemics change as they go: behavior, immunity, variants and reporting all shift, so yesterday's fit can mislead tomorrow. The data are measurements, not the epidemic: late, incomplete, and biased. A model calibrated in one place often travels badly to another. And a forecast is only honest if it was tested the way it will be used, with only the data available at the time.

transcript.title: Where the field is heading
transcript.text: Here's where I think the field is heading. Forecasts that adapt as conditions change: they notice when the regime shifts, and update only the parts that broke. Models that read many streams together, cases, wastewater, genomes and mobility, as views of one hidden epidemic, each with its own delays and biases. Language models that turn reports and bulletins into data, under strict checks, so that fluency is never mistaken for truth. And AI that helps epidemiologists, rather than trying to replace them. Shared benchmarks with archived data and their revisions, so that methods are compared fairly. And above all, models built around decisions, about beds, vaccines, testing and schools, rather than prediction for its own sake.

transcript.title: Thank you
transcript.text: If you've followed along, you can now build a model, fit it, question it, speed it up, and say how sure you are. That combination is rare, and the next epidemic will need it. Thank you for learning with me. Keep your models humble, your code tested, and your intervals honest. I'm Teddy, and this was Epidemic Modeling.

labs.title: Fitting an outbreak
labs.card: Fit one outbreak with four searches on a loss map, find the identifiability valley, and run ABC on a random town.
labs.text: Fit the module's simulated outbreak by weighted least squares with a grid, Nelder–Mead, gradient descent or a swarm, shorten the data to see the beta–gamma valley, and fit a stochastic town with ABC rejection.
labs.intro: The first panel fits the module's SIR outbreak and draws the loss over beta and gamma with each search's path; the second runs approximate Bayesian computation on a random outbreak in a town of 2,000. Everything runs in your browser.

labs.title: What surveillance sees
labs.card: Watch one hidden epidemic through reported cases, a serosurvey with imperfect tests, and wastewater samples.
labs.text: Change the reporting share and delay, correct a serosurvey for sensitivity and specificity, and see how noise, rain and sampling change what wastewater shows.
labs.intro: The module's simulated city runs in your browser: the true infections are known, and each panel shows what one data stream would see.

labs.title: Lockdowns and vaccine priority
labs.card: Slide a lockdown's start, length and strength against hospital beds and lost output, then choose who gets vaccinated first.
labs.text: Choose a lockdown's start day, length and strength in the module's town and see beds, deaths and lost output; then give a limited vaccine supply to children, adults or seniors first and compare infections and deaths.
labs.intro: The first panel runs the module's town of a million people with one lockdown you design; the second runs its age-structured version with a vaccine campaign. Everything runs in your browser.

labs.title: Sensitivity and forecast scores
labs.card: Rank the inputs of an SEIR model with local derivatives, Morris and Sobol, then score four forecasters for error, coverage and the weighted interval score.
labs.text: Run local, Morris and Sobol sensitivity analyses on the module's SEIR town, and backtest forecasters whose intervals you can stretch or shrink.
labs.intro: The first panel analyzes the module's SEIR town with seven uncertain inputs; the second backtests simple forecasters on a simulated epidemic. Everything runs in your browser.

labs.title: Step sizes and chance
labs.card: Solve the SIR model with Euler and Runge–Kutta, push a step until the epidemic goes negative, then compare exact and tau-leaping stochastic runs.
labs.text: Change the step size of Euler's method and of Runge–Kutta on the module's SIR town, and run hundreds of exact or tau-leaping stochastic outbreaks in towns of different sizes.
labs.intro: The first panel solves the module's SIR town with the step you choose and compares it with a solution made of tiny steps; the second runs 200 stochastic outbreaks, exactly or with tau-leaping. Everything runs in your browser.

games.title: Mayor's Outbreak
games.tagline: An SIR strategy game in your browser
games.text: Mayor's Outbreak is a browser-based SIR strategy simulation where you steer a city through an epidemic by balancing mobility, testing, and public protection.
